findings.quote: The Linux kernel, the C/C++ memory model, Python's runtime, and how a program becomes a process. Compilers, linkers, system calls, and the shape of an operating system.
findings.problem: Part II does not teach most of what this line lists. "The C/C++ memory model" is a standard term for atomics and memory ordering (std::atomic, memory_order). The book teaches that in Part V (Ch16 §03, Fig 16.5), and the phrase never appears in part-2.html. Part II actually teaches pointers, manual memory, undefined behaviour and RAII. "How a program becomes a process" gets only one strip line (Fig 4.10, fork then execve). Linkers get one clause in ch7-interpret. System calls are taught mainly in Part I's Bridge (chBridge-trap). The part-2 page's own chapter lines are accurate, so the cover now promises a different Part II than the page delivers.
findings.fix: Rewrite the line from what Part II covers, for example: "The kernel as a real program: scheduling, virtual memory, filesystems, IPC. C's pointers, manual memory and undefined behaviour; C++'s classes and RAII; Python's interpreter and the GIL."

findings.quote: The place where the book has to begin.
findings.problem: This sentence fragment does no job (law 2) and contradicts the same page. The footer says "A self-contained book · open any part to begin" and the meta line says SELF-CONTAINED; Pass 23 (§4w) confirmed that "open any part" is true. A careful reader sees "has to begin" here and "any part" below and stops to work out which is meant. It also cuts down part-1's own intro line ("This is where the story has to begin: in the place most books skip") into a slogan.
findings.fix: Cut the sentence. If the shelf needs a closer, say what Part I is to the rest without telling the reader where to start, for example "The bottom layer every later part stands on."

findings.quote: Transistors, Boolean algebra, IEEE 754, the CPU, assembly, buffer overflows, and the hardware face of the kernel.
findings.problem: "IEEE 754" is a standard's number, and a newcomer on the cover cannot tell it means floating-point numbers. The section that teaches it is called "Floating point". "The hardware face of the kernel" is also opaque before the reader has seen the Bridge, which glosses it.
findings.fix: Use "floating-point numbers" for "IEEE 754", and "the hardware every kernel depends on" (or similar) for "the hardware face of the kernel".

findings.quote: CH 1–3 + BRIDGE
findings.problem: The shelf placard under volume I in the wide SVG exhibit says "CH 1–3 + BRIDGE". The same hero at phone width says "CH 1–3 · BRIDGE", and the shelves say "CHAPTERS 1 TO 3 · BRIDGE". So the Part I label changes with the viewport.
findings.fix: Make the SVG placard read "CH 1–3 · BRIDGE" to match the stacked bar and the shelves.

findings.quote: <meta property="og:image:alt" content="Under the Code: a transistor on the left, a globe on the right, a thin gold arc between them.">
findings.problem: This alt text describes the old cover art. The current og-image.png and og-image.svg show concentric dashed rings around one transistor in the centre, with the wordmark and "FROM TRANSISTOR TO CIVILIZATION · EIGHTEEN CHAPTERS" below. There is no globe and no arc. Screen readers read this text aloud in every social preview of the book's link.
findings.fix: Describe the image as it is: "Under the Code: a gold transistor at the centre of concentric rings, above the title and 'From transistor to civilization'."

findings.quote: C++: When C Needed to Think in Objects / Packets: How the Internet Decided to Work
findings.problem: The cover's contents and the part pages' chapter lists use normal title case. The chapter heroes for the same chapters read "When C Needed To Think In Objects" (ch6-hero-title) and "Packets: How The Internet Decided to Work" (ch9-hero-title). In those, "In" and "The" are capitalised mid-title, while "Decided to Work" leaves "to" lower case. So a chapter's title is cased differently on the cover and on its own opening page.
findings.fix: Keep the cover as is. Lower-case "to", "in" and "the" in the two hero h1s so they match the cover (the line breaks can stay).

findings.quote: The ACID guarantee that a transaction beginning in a valid database state ends in one, with referential integrity, constraints and data types intact.
findings.problem: book.js puts this tooltip on every / whose text matches the key, outside the defining section. ch17-cap marks Consistency (part-5.html line 1968), "(every read returns the most recent write)", so the CAP theorem's Consistency gets the ACID definition. The tooltip contradicts the sentence it sits in, and mixing up ACID's C with CAP's C is exactly the confusion a newcomer is prone to. Second problem: "referential integrity" appears nowhere in the book. The section explains the idea in plain words: "every order still belongs to a customer who exists, every amount is a number".
findings.fix: In ACID, the guarantee that a transaction beginning in a valid database state ends in one, with the database's rules intact (every order still belongs to a customer who exists). In the CAP theorem the word means something else: every read returns the most recent write.

findings.quote: current flows from collector to emitter while the base carries a voltage
findings.problem: Fig 1.4's strip says the dots are "Electrons, drifting from emitter to collector". The tooltip gives the opposite direction. Both are right, since conventional current runs opposite to electron flow, but the book never teaches that, so a careful reader sees a contradiction. The section's text gives no direction at all, only "a much larger current flow between the other two".
findings.fix: One of a transistor's two current-carrying terminals, the emitter being the other (in the field-effect design the drain plays its part); while the base carries a small voltage, current flows between collector and emitter.

findings.quote: for two decades the most common web vulnerability
findings.problem: The section says "one of the most common web vulnerabilities for two decades running". The glossary turns that into a claim that XSS was the single most common, which is not true. On the OWASP Top 10, XSS was first only in 2007; it was third in 2010 and 2013, seventh in 2017, and folded into Injection in 2021 (sources: cs.ru.nl/E.Poll/talks/OWASP_Top_Ten.pdf, therecord.media on the OWASP ranking, infosecinstitute.com 2013 vs 2017). The sibling entry `xss` repeats the same overstatement.
findings.fix: An attack that injects the attacker's script into a site's own pages, so it runs with that origin's full privileges; one of the most common web vulnerabilities for two decades.

findings.quote: a block-cipher mode that turns AES into a stream cipher
findings.problem: "Stream cipher" appears nowhere in the book, and neither does "block cipher", so the definition explains the term with words the reader was never given. The section says only: counter mode, AES encrypting a running counter.
findings.fix: Counter mode: a mode of operation in which AES encrypts a running counter (1, 2, 3 and on) and the result is XORed with the plaintext, so repeated plaintext blocks still come out different.

findings.quote: the connection ID lives at the application level, so a phone switching from Wi-Fi to cellular keeps its connection
findings.problem: Migration does not work because of where the ID "lives". It works because the ID, not the address-and-port pair, names the connection, which is how the section puts it: "a connection ID, not the address pair, names the connection". "Lives at the application level" gives the wrong cause, and a reader may also take it to mean the ID belongs to HTTP rather than to QUIC's own packets.
findings.fix: A QUIC feature: each connection is named by a connection ID instead of the address and port pair, so a phone switching from Wi-Fi to mobile data keeps its connection, which TCP, tied to addresses and ports, cannot.

findings.quote: how ZFS, btrfs and APFS never overwrite blocks
findings.problem: The section qualifies APFS: "copy-on-write filesystems like ZFS, btrfs and (for its metadata) Apple's APFS never overwrite existing data", and its strip repeats that APFS checksums cover only metadata. The glossary drops the qualifier and claims APFS never overwrites any block. Apple's own guide describes a copy-on-write metadata scheme.
findings.fix: Sharing data read-only and making a private copy only when something writes to it: how fork() avoids duplicating memory, and how ZFS, btrfs and (for its metadata) APFS never overwrite blocks in place.

findings.quote: checks at run time that every indirect call or return targets an address the compiler judged valid
findings.problem: The defining section, ch15-memory-p3, says CFI "adds a check before every indirect call" and then: "Returns are guarded by the shadow stack and Pointer Authentication below." The tooltip says CFI also checks returns, which contradicts the paragraph it defines. The sibling `cfi` entry has the same wording.
findings.fix: A defence, proposed by Martín Abadi and colleagues in 2005 and now built into major compilers, that checks before each indirect call that the target is one the compiler recorded as valid for that call site; returns are guarded separately, by shadow stacks and Pointer Authentication.

findings.quote: refusing writes rather than risk disagreement
findings.problem: In the section, a CP system "refuses to serve requests on the wrong side of the split", and Fig 17.7's CP replica refuses a read ("read x? error: can't confirm"). Limiting the refusal to writes contradicts the figure the reader has just seen.
findings.fix: Distributed stores that choose consistency during a partition: a replica that cannot confirm the latest value refuses the request rather than answer with stale data, as etcd, ZooKeeper and Google Spanner do.

findings.quote: bytecode for a stack-based virtual machine
findings.problem: Ch4 (ch4-security) defines a virtual machine as something that "imitates an entire computer, kernel and all, on a hypervisor". Here the term is used in a different sense, for an interpreter that runs bytecode, and the reader is not told. The section itself deliberately says "a stack machine, which computes on the values at the top of a stack".
findings.fix: A program that translates source code into a lower-level form: machine code for C, or, inside CPython, bytecode for a stack machine that CPython's eval loop then runs.

findings.quote: One program runs always.
findings.problem: This brings back an error that §4g fixed. The ledger row 'Glossary "kernel": "the one program that always runs"' says the kernel is resident, not running, while a user process runs (OSTEP 6.3). The glossary was corrected, and ch1-kernel-p4 now says 'the one program that stays loaded'. The Ch4 hero puts the old wording back in the first line of the chapter.
findings.fix: "One program stays loaded from power-on to shutdown." (the rest of the lead unchanged)

findings.quote: where voltage on copper becomes voltage across a continent
findings.problem: This brings back an error that §4g fixed in its Fig 8.1 row: long-distance links carry light in glass fibre, not voltage. Part III's own Fig 8.1 and ch8-substrates now show light in fibre over 5,600 km. A reader who goes on to Part III meets the correction on its first page.
findings.fix: "where a voltage on copper becomes light in glass fibre crossing an ocean."

findings.quote: By 1979, C was running million-line systems and the seams were showing.
findings.problem: This cannot be verified, and the chapter itself does not support it. This is the open §4o flag: V7 UNIX was about 10^5 lines, and 5ESS dates from 1982 on. ch6-complexity-p2 credits the million-line projects of the time to OS/360 (written in assembly) and Multics (PL/I), not to C. ch5-survives-p6 and Stroustrup's own account give his motive as Simula's organisation against BCPL/C speed from his thesis work, not C codebases breaking (cplusplus.com/info/history).
findings.fix: "By 1979, programs were outgrowing what one team could hold in its head, and C offered only the function to organise them with."

findings.quote: you give up an order of magnitude of performance
findings.problem: The figure disagrees with the rest of the part, which is the open §4o flag. The part ending says 'slower than C by orders of magnitude'. ch7-interpret-p3 says 'hundreds of CPU instructions' per statement, ch7-datasci-p5 says 'a hundred machine cycles', and Fig 7.9 shows about ten thousand times. A reader sees two different sizes for the same trade.
findings.fix: "you give up one to two orders of magnitude of performance" (or "often a factor of ten to a hundred")

findings.quote: Before C, every operating system was rewritten from scratch for every machine. The cost was civilizational.
findings.problem: 'Every' goes further than the chapter. ch5-portability-p1 says 'usually'. ch5-portability-p2 itself describes System/360 as a family of machines sharing their systems software. Burroughs MCP (1961, ESPOL) and Multics (PL/I) were written in high-level languages. 'The cost was civilizational.' is also a clipped dramatic fragment.
findings.fix: "Before C, an operating system was usually written in assembly for one machine and rewritten for the next, at a civilizational cost." (this keeps the owner's word)

findings.quote: C++, the object-oriented answer to its complexity;
findings.problem: 'Its' reads as UNIX's or C's complexity. Chapter 6 says the opposite: C was too simple, offering only the function (ch6-complexity-p3), while programs grew too large to manage. C++ answered the complexity of large programs, not of C.
findings.fix: "C++, the object-oriented answer to programs grown too large for C;"

findings.quote: That language now runs trading systems, game engines, browsers, and most of your operating system's user-space.
findings.problem: 'Most of your operating system's user-space' is not true for most readers. Linux user space is mostly C (glibc, coreutils, systemd), macOS is largely C, Objective-C and Swift, and Android user space is largely Java and Kotlin. The chapter body (ch6-stroustrup-p3) lists trading platforms, telecom switches, browser engines and game runtimes, with no OS claim. ch5-survives-p1 calls the OS layer C.
findings.fix: "That language now runs trading systems, game engines, browsers and telephone switches."

findings.quote: The answer was not a new language. It was C with classes added on top,
findings.problem: This is a 'Not X. Y.' reveal, and it is also wrong by the chapter's own account. The language was renamed C++ in 1983 and standardised in 1998 (ch6-stroustrup-p3), and the ch5-survives strip calls C++ only 'nearly' a superset of C. The next sentence then calls it 'That language'.
findings.fix: "His answer was C with classes added on top, in a way that costs you nothing if you don't use them."

findings.quote: The kernel as code, not silicon. C, the language UNIX rewrote itself in. ... Three different deals with the same machine. All three still in production. All three necessary, for different reasons, for different problems.
findings.problem: This is a run of verbless fragments ending in a triple 'All three' anaphora and the filler pair 'for different reasons, for different problems'. It mostly restates the part opener, almost word for word in 'Part I built the substrate; Part II opened the program that owns it' (law 2). 'Three different deals' comes right after a list of four items (kernel plus three languages). The other closers are two or three sentences.
findings.fix: "Part II read the kernel as code, then three languages that strike different deals with the same machine: C stays close to it, C++ scales it to systems too big for one head, and Python trades orders of magnitude of speed for readability, handing its fast parts to C. All three are still in production."

findings.quote: Without it, modern computing is impossible: no multitasking, no security, no internet. This is the kernel.
findings.problem: 'This is the kernel.' is a reveal closer after a run of short dramatic sentences ('Every other program lives at its mercy.'). 'No internet' overclaims: microcontrollers run TCP/IP stacks such as lwIP on bare metal with no kernel.
findings.fix: "Without it there is no multitasking and no protection between programs. It is the kernel."

findings.quote: It is, once again, a story about people: Shannon, Baran, Davies, Cerf, Berners-Lee, Eich. And it is, once again, a story about silicon and the abstractions we build over it.
findings.problem: Two parallel 'It is, once again' sentences. The second calls Part III a story about silicon, but Part III is about the network. Cerf is named without Kahn, although Part III credits the 1974 protocol paper to 'Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn'.
findings.fix: "Its people are Shannon, Baran, Davies, Cerf and Kahn, Berners-Lee and Eich." Drop the silicon sentence.

findings.quote: End of Part Two
findings.problem: The other closers read 'End of Part I', 'End of Part III' and 'End of Part IV'. The headline 'The kernel and the languages.' also breaks the '... is built.' pattern of the other four closers. Pass 19 flagged both and they are still open; neither is a §5 non-defect.
findings.fix: "End of Part II". Headline, if the owner wants the pattern: "The software layer is built."

findings.quote: 05 · Undefined behavior
findings.problem: The Ch5 tab and section label spell it 'behavior'. The part opener ('undefined behaviour') and six places in the chapter's own prose spell it 'behaviour', so a reader sees the section's own term spelled two ways.
findings.fix: Pick one spelling for the term throughout Part II, e.g. "05 · Undefined behaviour" in the tab and label.

findings.quote: Scheduler · VM · FS · IPC · Security / Portability · Pointers · UB · The systems contract / the GIL
findings.problem: The topic previews are bare acronyms a newcomer cannot read before the chapter: VM, FS, IPC, UB, GIL, RAII. 'VM' also collides with 'virtual machine', which Ch17 teaches. The section tabs next to them spell the same things out ('Virtual memory', 'Filesystems', 'Undefined behavior').
findings.fix: "Scheduler · Virtual memory · Filesystems · IPC · Security"; "Portability · Pointers · Undefined behaviour · The systems contract"; "The GIL (global interpreter lock)" in the Ch7 Topics line and TOC.

findings.quote: Era covered 1969 → present (Ch5) · Era covered 1979 → present (Ch6)
findings.problem: Both chapters start their history earlier than their stated era. Ch5 §01 opens with System/360 (1965) and BCPL (1967). Ch6's own timeline (Fig 6.2) starts at Simula 67, and §01 at Brooks (1975). Smaller cases: Ch4 teaches Little's law (1961) and Dijkstra's semaphores (1965); Ch7 opens with Lisp (1959).
findings.fix: Ch5 "1965 → present"; Ch6 "1967 → present" (Ch4 and Ch7 can stay as the eras of their subjects).

findings.quote: The machine that runs nearly all code in 2026 is not a computer at all but a great many computers: sixteen cores in your laptop, sixty-four in a cloud server, ten thousand machines in a region
findings.problem: Sixteen cores in one laptop are one computer, not "a great many computers". The part contradicts itself here: ch16-numa-p5 says "Parallelism scales the single computer up", and only after that come "many computers, sharing no memory" (Ch17). A reader of the opener learns that cores and machines are the same kind of thing, and Ch16 then has to undo it. The sentence is also the "not X but Y" reveal pattern.
findings.fix: Separate the two scales, e.g. "The machine that runs nearly all code in 2026 is many processors working as one: sixteen cores in your laptop, sixty-four in a cloud server, and beyond them ten thousand machines in a region, tied together by software that must reach agreement despite delay and failure."

findings.quote: Around 2004 the clock speed of consumer CPUs stopped rising (heat density made it impossible)
findings.problem: Overclaim. Clock-speed growth collapsed, but clocks did not stop. Intel's fastest part in late 2004 was the 3.8 GHz Pentium 4 570J; the Core i9-13900KS (2023) reached 6.0 GHz and the i9-14900KS (2024) 6.2 GHz boost (Intel newsroom, "i9-14900KS Powers Desktop PCs to Record-Breaking Speeds"; AnandTech on the 570J and on Tejas being cancelled for heat). A reader whose machine boosts past 5 GHz will stop here. "Impossible" is too strong: further rises became too costly, not impossible.
findings.fix: "Around 2004 the clock speed of consumer CPUs nearly stopped rising (heat density made each further step too costly)"

findings.quote: The cloud is the substrate of nearly every web service, every mobile backend, every AI training run, every database larger than a laptop.
findings.problem: "Every database larger than a laptop" is false. Gartner puts about 36% of 2024 DBMS spending still on premises (cloud about 64%; 2021: just over 49%). Banks, governments and the large AI labs' own clusters (Meta, national-lab supercomputers) run outside anyone else's cloud. The sentence just before says "someone else's datacenter", so a reader takes it literally.
findings.fix: Scope it, e.g. "The cloud now carries most web services and mobile back ends, much of AI training, and a growing majority of large databases."

findings.quote: It is built from a handful of layered abstractions: virtualization, containers, orchestration, consensus protocols, service meshes. Each of them solves a problem the layer below could not.
findings.problem: Consensus is not a layer above orchestration. The chapter shows the reverse: Kubernetes keeps its state in etcd, which runs Raft (Fig 17.3 strip; ch17-consensus-p1, "Kubernetes' 'source of truth', etcd, runs ... Raft"). Read as a stack, the list puts consensus on top of Kubernetes, and "the layer below" points the wrong way.
findings.fix: Drop the stacking claim, or reorder: "It is built from a handful of abstractions: virtualization, containers, orchestration resting on consensus protocols, and service meshes. Each solves a problem the ones before it could not."

findings.quote: Most code in 2026 runs in someone else's datacenter, on hardware its developers will never touch
findings.problem: No measure is given or supportable. Phones, laptops and embedded devices run vast amounts of code. The part opener a page earlier also counts "sixteen cores in your laptop" as where code runs.
findings.fix: "Most web services in 2026 run in someone else's datacenter, ..." (or "Much of the code behind the services you use").

findings.quote: coordinating across a network that is unreliable in ways that look like physics
findings.problem: A newcomer cannot work out what "in ways that look like physics" means: delay, loss or partitions? The chapter later names the real failures: messages delayed or lost, machines crashing, partitions.
findings.fix: "coordinating across a network that delays, drops and cuts off messages without warning"

findings.quote: Writing code that uses them correctly is one of the deepest skills in programming, and its failure modes are some of the most frustrating bugs ever produced.
findings.problem: A superlative pair that teaches nothing (law 2). It also says failure modes "are" bugs, and "ever produced" is unsupported. The chapter's real point is that these bugs depend on timing and hide in testing (Fig 16.2 strip, "Why it hides").
findings.fix: "Writing code that uses them correctly is hard: its bugs depend on timing, hide in testing and appear under load."

findings.quote: A single CPU, with its kernel, speaking through one network stack to one TLS endpoint, holding bytes in one relational database, defended by a layered stack we can now name.
findings.problem: A verbless fragment standing as a sentence. Its last clause uses "a layered stack" to mean defence in depth, in the same sentence where "network stack" means something else, so the reader cannot tell which stack defends the machine.
findings.fix: Join it to the previous sentence with a colon, and name the defence: "Parts I through IV built one computer: a single CPU and its kernel, speaking through one network stack to one TLS endpoint, holding bytes in one relational database, guarded by layered defences (Chapter 15)."

findings.quote: Era covered~1965 → present (Ch16 and Ch17 heroes)
findings.problem: Both chapters show the same approximate start, and neither covers anything from 1965. Ch16's earliest event is Amdahl's 1967 paper (ch16-amdahl-p1); Ch17's is CP/CMS in 1968 (ch17-virt-p1; §4g: CP-40 1967, CP/CMS shipped 1968). Every other chapter gives an exact year it actually starts from (1936, 1847, 1949, ...), so the matching "~1965" reads like a placeholder.
findings.fix: Ch16: "1967 → present"; Ch17: "1968 → present".

findings.quote: Seventeen chapters ago this book began with a single transistor: a switch made of doped silicon, controlled by voltage, doing nothing on its own.
findings.problem: The book did not begin with a transistor. Chapter 1 opens with human computers and Turing's 1936 machine (ch1-context, era 1936 → 1974); the transistor arrives in its Section 02. A reader who remembers the opening will notice. ch18-final-p6 says it accurately: "Chapter 1 drew a single transistor."
findings.fix: "Seventeen chapters ago this book drew a single transistor: ..." or "The stack this book built starts with a single transistor: ..."

findings.quote: The computer is no longer a thing. It is a layered system that runs everywhere, holds nearly all knowledge produced by humans, and increasingly shapes the decisions of every domain it touches.
findings.problem: This is the "Not X. Y." reveal followed by a reflexive triplet. "Holds nearly all knowledge produced by humans" overreaches. What is true is that nearly all stored information is now digital (Hilbert and López, Science 2011: 94% of storage capacity by 2007). Knowledge in general, including undigitised archives and books, is not.
findings.fix: "The computer has become a layered system that runs nearly everywhere, stores nearly all the information we record, and shapes decisions in every field it touches."

findings.quote: This chapter does no new teaching.
findings.problem: The chapter does teach new material. ch18-future-p1 introduces neuromorphic and analog accelerators and specialised chips, which no earlier chapter covers. ch18-intersect brings in AlphaFold and the genome project, and ch18-reading is new. The lead itself goes on to say the chapter "points at where the field is going".
findings.fix: "This chapter adds little new: it looks back at the whole, names what's permanent and what isn't, points at where the field is going, and ends."

findings.quote: Clusterone curriculum · five layers · one reader
findings.problem: The chapter's first figure counts the layers differently. Fig 18.1's picture says "The book's eleven layers", transistor to distributed systems. The five are the book's parts (the final figure's rings are transistor, CPU, kernel, network, cloud, civilization). A reader meets "five layers" and then "eleven layers" a few screens apart.
findings.fix: "one curriculum · five parts · one reader"

findings.quote: From a single transistor in 1947 to a planet-scale distributed service in 2026.
findings.problem: The book's own history starts earlier. Fig 18.2's timeline (ch18-civilization) begins with Boole in 1854 and Turing in 1936; Chapter 2's era starts in 1847 and Chapter 1's in 1936. Read as a date range, the closer contradicts the timeline the reader saw minutes before.
findings.fix: Make it the stack, not the dates: "From a single transistor to a planet-scale distributed service." Or keep dates that match Fig 18.2: "From Boole's algebra in 1854 to a planet-scale distributed service in 2026."

findings.quote: Check your email. The link works for 24 hours. Nothing is created until you click it.
findings.problem: This is the account page status line after 'Send confirmation link' (account.html:574). It is false. signup goes through signupMail, which calls ensureUser (functions/api/auth/_account.js), and that INSERTs the users row (email, created_at) as soon as the form is submitted, before anyone clicks. The privacy notice on the same page contradicts it too: 'an account whose email is never confirmed is removed after 14 days'.
findings.fix: Check your email. The link works for 24 hours. Until you click it, we hold only your address, and we remove it after 14 days.

findings.quote: Pick one now; you can add the other any time below.
findings.problem: Production has passkeys off (meta utc-passkeys="off", PASSKEYS_ENABLED="0"). The JS hides the passkey button and the passkey list, so a new reader who has just confirmed sees 'Choose how you'll sign in' and only one button, 'Set a password'. There is no 'other' to pick or add below. Other strings that stay visible offer the same missing option: 'Email links are retiring' + 'Choose how you'll sign in next time: a passkey or a password.'; the recover setup line 'Set a new password, or create a passkey, so next time you won't need an email.'; the recover help 'Once in, you can set a password or create a passkey.' and the create help 'then you choose how you'll sign in'.
findings.fix: While passkeysOn is false, switch these strings in the JS. setup-title: 'Set a password.'; setup-help: 'You can change it any time below.'; retiring help: 'Set a password for next time. Your reading position stays exactly where it is.'; recover help: 'Once in, you can set a password.'; create help: 'We send one link to confirm it; then you set a password.' Keep the current wording for when passkeys are switched on.

findings.quote: Where it lives: a Cloudflare D1 database in the European Union
findings.problem: The database does not guarantee this. Running `wrangler d1 info under-book` gives jurisdiction: null and running_in_region: EEUR. EEUR is a location hint, not a jurisdiction. Cloudflare's D1 data-location page says: 'Providing a location hint does not guarantee that D1 runs in your preferred location', and it does not define 'Eastern Europe' as EU-only. Only the 'eu' jurisdiction, which can only be set when a database is created, guarantees the data runs and is stored in the EU (https://developers.cloudflare.com/d1/configuration/data-location/). A privacy notice states this as fact.
findings.fix: Owner's call. Either recreate the database with --jurisdiction=eu, migrate the data, and keep the sentence; or make the text match the setup: 'a Cloudflare D1 database placed in Cloudflare's Eastern Europe region, the same infrastructure that already serves the book.'

findings.quote: Expired records are swept automatically every few hours.
findings.problem: There is no scheduled sweep. maybeCleanup (functions/api/_lib.js:289-317) runs only when a request hits signup, recover or login, and at most once every 6 hours. On a quiet site nothing is swept for as long as nobody signs in or up. That means unconfirmed accounts can outlive the promised 14 days and counters can outlive 'about a day'. The notice describes a schedule the code does not run.
findings.fix: Expired records are swept the next time anyone signs in or signs up, at most six hours apart. (Or add a cron Worker and keep the sentence.)

findings.quote: and when it was last updated. ... cleared after about a day. Nothing else.
findings.problem: The list ends with 'Nothing else.', but the schema stores more. users.created_at (when the account was requested) and password_updated_at. For each passkey, its credential ID, signature counter, transports and a synced flag (migrations/0001_accounts_v2.sql). Each emailed-link record also holds a return path, and a per-account 'nudge:<user id>' counter (login.js:60) is keyed by the account id, not 'a keyed hash of the address or network'. 'Nothing else.' also appears twice in adjacent bullets as a clipped closing fragment.
findings.fix: Add 'when the account was created and the password last changed' and 'for each passkey, its ID and the counters the passkey standard needs'. Keep a single 'Nothing else.', at the end of the list only.

findings.quote: An account adds exactly one thing: the same reading position, stored server-side so it can follow you between devices. In detail:
findings.problem: The bullets that follow straight away list an email, a password hash, passkeys, session hashes, link and challenge records and counters, as well as the position. 'Exactly one thing' contradicts the detail it introduces.
findings.fix: An account adds the same reading position, stored server-side so it can follow you between devices, and what is needed to sign you in. In detail:

findings.quote: Your address receives only the links you yourself request and a short notice whenever your sign-in settings change
findings.problem: Two other mails can arrive. If anyone tries to create an account with a confirmed address, signupMail sends the 'You already have an account' notice, which you did not request and which is not a settings change. An email-link-era reader who tries a password is sent a sign-in link automatically (login.js nudge).
findings.fix: ...the links you yourself request, a short notice whenever your sign-in settings change, and a notice if someone tries to create an account with your address: no announcements, no marketing.

findings.quote: Some passages offer an optional outside video.
findings.problem: The whole book has exactly one video aside (public/part-1.html:235, data-yt="JsBZOcqZerk", the Enigma video). 'Some passages' overstates it.
findings.fix: One passage offers an optional outside video. (Change it back to 'Some' when more are added.)

findings.quote: Deletion: the button above removes your email, password, passkeys, sessions and position immediately and completely.
findings.problem: The notice is shown to signed-out readers as well, and above it they see only the sign-in form. The Delete account button exists only in the signed-in block, so 'the button above' points at nothing.
findings.fix: Deletion: the Delete account button (shown above once you are signed in) removes your email, password, passkeys, sessions and position immediately and completely.

findings.quote: 'Signed out on ' + res.data.ended + ' other ' + 'session'/'sessions' + '.'  (renders e.g. "Signed out on 2 other sessions.")
findings.problem: The 'Sign out everywhere else' result reads 'Signed out on 2 other sessions.' The 'on' fits devices, not sessions, so the line is ungrammatical.
findings.fix: 'Ended ' + n + ' other ' + (n === 1 ? 'session' : 'sessions') + '.' (e.g. 'Ended 2 other sessions.')

findings.quote: The book has five parts, an index, and a glossary. Every other path is undefined.
findings.problem: The book has no index. The link row right below offers 'cover', not 'index' (index.html is the cover), so a reader goes looking for an index that does not exist. '/account' is another real path, which makes 'Every other path is undefined' false. That closer is also a quip-style aphorism.
findings.fix: The book has a cover, five parts and a glossary. (Drop the closing sentence, or make it 'The links below lead back in.')

findings.quote: chosen by NIST in 2001
findings.problem: Brings back an error the §4g ledger already corrected (Part IV verification row: NIST chose Rijndael on 2 October 2000 and published FIPS 197 in November 2001). It also contradicts its own defining paragraph, ch14-symmetric-p1, which says NIST chose it in 2000 and published it as the standard in 2001.
findings.fix: The Advanced Encryption Standard: the symmetric block cipher Rijndael, by Vincent Rijmen and Joan Daemen, chosen by NIST in 2000 and published as the standard in 2001. It does the bulk encryption in nearly every modern system.

findings.quote: which ignores loss as a signal and instead measures bandwidth and RTT
findings.problem: Says flatly, in the present tense, that BBR ignores loss. The §4g Fig 10.8 row corrected exactly this ('loss-agnostic'): only the first version largely ignored loss, and later versions (BBRv2, v3) react to it. The defining section's own strip says so: 'The first BBR largely ignored loss; later versions react to it too.'
findings.fix: Bottleneck Bandwidth and Round-trip propagation time: Google's 2016 congestion control, which measures the bottleneck's bandwidth and the shortest round trip and keeps about one bandwidth-delay product in flight, instead of waiting for loss. The first version largely ignored loss; later ones react to it too.

findings.quote: and the level BBR tries to hold its window at
findings.problem: This is a softened form of 'BBR keeps cwnd at exactly BDP', which the §4g Fig 10.8 row corrected to 'keeps about one BDP in flight while probing above and below it'. BBR's congestion window is in fact about twice the BDP (cwnd_gain 2). Pacing is what holds the data in flight near one BDP. The strip in ch10-modern says 'keeps about one BDP in flight', not the window.
findings.fix: Bandwidth times round-trip time: the amount of data in flight that fills a network path exactly without anything waiting in its buffers, and the amount BBR tries to keep in flight.

findings.quote: made precise by Jim Gray
findings.problem: Gives the acronym's precision to Gray alone. Gray's 1981 paper set out the transaction concept, and Theo Härder and Andreas Reuter named and framed ACID in 1983. The defining section's own strip says so ('Jim Gray set out the transaction concept in 1981; Theo Härder and Andreas Reuter named it ACID in 1983'), so the tooltip contradicts the figure next to it.
findings.fix: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability: the four guarantees a relational database makes about its transactions. Jim Gray set out the transaction concept in 1981, and Theo Härder and Andreas Reuter named it ACID in 1983.

findings.quote: the first practical public-key system
findings.problem: The same section, ch14-publickey-p1, opens with the 1976 Diffie–Hellman protocol, a practical public-key scheme a year older than RSA. A reader who has just read that will stop at 'first'. RSA's real first is narrower: the first practical public-key system for encryption and signatures.
findings.fix: Leonard Adleman, who with Ron Rivest and Adi Shamir at MIT published RSA in 1977, the first practical public-key system for encrypting and signing (Diffie–Hellman, a year earlier, only agrees a key).

findings.quote: "section": "ch7-datasci"
findings.problem: The entry is filed under ch7-datasci, so its glossary link reads 'Chapter 7 · §06 →' and lands on 'Why Python won data science', which never names Baran. The build script's section finder picked up the only earlier mention, the plain-text Part II closing tagline ('Shannon, Baran, Davies, ...'), which sits after that section. Baran is taught in ch9-arpanet (p2, Fig 9.3), and the definition is correct against that section.
findings.fix: Keep the definition: 'Paul Baran of the RAND Corporation, who between 1960 and 1964 argued for a survivable mesh network with no centre, its messages broken into independently routed blocks.' File it under ch9-arpanet (Chapter 9 · §02), where he is taught, so the link leads to him.

findings.quote: while the compiler turns it into a Promise chain underneath
findings.problem: The defining section says 'the engine runs it on Promises underneath', and its strip says each await pauses the function, which then continues as a microtask. Engines do not rewrite an async function into a .then chain. They suspend and resume it. 'Compiler' and 'Promise chain' give a different, less accurate picture than the section teaches.
findings.fix: JavaScript syntax (ES2017) that lets asynchronous code be written as if it were synchronous: each await pauses the function until its Promise settles, and the engine resumes it as a microtask, running on Promises underneath.

findings.quote: (the gate, in the modern field-effect design): a small voltage here lets a much larger current flow between collector and emitter
findings.problem: Mixes the two transistor kinds in one sentence. After naming the field-effect gate, it puts the current between collector and emitter, which belong to the older bipolar kind. ch1-transistor-p7 and Fig 1.5 teach that in a field-effect transistor the current runs between source and drain.
findings.fix: The control terminal of the older, bipolar transistor: a small voltage here lets a much larger current flow between collector and emitter. In the field-effect transistors of modern chips the gate plays this part, between source and drain.

findings.quote: element i sits i sizes past the start
findings.problem: 'i sizes' is unclear wording, and it quietly assumes counting from zero, which a Chapter 3 newcomer has not been told. Read literally, element 1 would not be the first value.
findings.fix: A row of same-sized values stored one after another in memory, reached by position: counting from 0, element i sits i times the value's size past the start.

findings.quote: the cryptography that makes the web possible at all
findings.problem: The book itself contradicts this. Ch11 shows the web running in cleartext from 1989 (ch11-crypto-p1: every protocol so far is cleartext, and that was acceptable for years), and ch15-network-p3 talks about 'the non-TLS web of the 1990s and 2000s'. Cryptography makes the web trustworthy. The web was possible without it.
findings.fix: the cryptography that lets a browser trust a server it has never met

findings.quote: the relational database that organises every record in production
findings.problem: 'Every record' is false, and Ch13 says so: ch13-injection-p7 discusses NoSQL systems, and a lot of production data lives in key-value stores, document stores, object storage and files.
findings.fix: the relational database that still organises most of the records in production

findings.quote: Part IV is about the bytes themselves once they stop moving: how information is stored so that it can be queried, how it is encrypted so that it can be trusted,
findings.problem: This misdescribes the part. Ch14 builds up to the TLS handshake, which protects bytes in transit (DH key agreement, Fig 14.11), and Ch15 Section 03 is about network attacks and MITM. So most of the part is about bytes that are moving. 'Encrypted so that it can be trusted' also goes against what Ch14 teaches: encryption alone gives secrecy, and trust comes from signatures, certificates and authentication tags. ch14-symmetric-p4 even says CBC does not detect tampering.
findings.fix: Part IV is about the bytes themselves: how information is stored so that it can be queried, how cryptography keeps it secret and proves where it came from, and how the systems that hold it can be attacked and defended.

findings.quote: SQL is also the most attacked surface on the modern internet.
findings.problem: Unsupported superlative, and the chapter's own body hedges it ('one of the most damaging vulnerability classes', ch13-injection-p1). OWASP Top 10:2025 puts Injection fifth, behind Broken Access Control (owasp.org/Top10/2025/0x00_2025-Introduction/). Akamai's '~65% of web-app attacks are SQLi' figure covers 2017-19, and by 2022 Local File Inclusion had overtaken it in the commerce sector (darkreading.com, akamai.com newsroom). It also sits at the end as a one-line dramatic closer.
findings.fix: SQL injection (Section 06) remains one of the most damaging attacks on the web.

findings.quote: Post-quantum standardisation. The math made physical.
findings.problem: The last item in Ch14's topic line points to nothing in the chapter. No section covers hardware or physical implementation. The phrase is Ch18's closing theme (part-5 h2 'Every layer is math made physical'), so it reads as a slogan borrowed from elsewhere. Meanwhile Section 06, TLS 1.3 at cryptographic depth, is left out of the line.
findings.fix: Replace with: "TLS 1.3 read at full depth."

findings.quote: The theory is set theory; the practice is fifty years of refinement; the surface area is small enough that a working programmer can master it in weeks.
findings.problem: A reflexive triplet of parallel clauses. 'Master it in weeks' is also an overclaim next to the chapter's own isolation levels, MVCC and query planning, which take years to master.
findings.fix: Its theory is set theory, and its core is small enough to learn in weeks.

findings.quote: SQL is the first language in this book that tells the computer what you want, and leaves the how to a query planner.
findings.problem: Ch12 already showed declarative code: React-style frameworks where 'the programmer writes declarative rules ("the page should look like X"); the framework computes the minimum set of DOM mutations' (part-3, ch12-dom), along with HTML and CSS parsed into trees. A careful reader coming from Ch12 will notice that the 'first' claim is wrong.
findings.fix: SQL instead tells the computer what you want, and leaves the how to a query planner.

findings.quote: Cryptography is the only mathematics in this book whose entire purpose is to be computationally hard to reverse.
findings.problem: An aphorism closer. It is also imprecise against the chapter: AES decryption is meant to be easy for the key holder (ch14-primer-p1 says AES rests on no one-way function), and the one-time pad in Fig 14.1's strip is information-theoretically secure, not computationally hard.
findings.fix: Cut the sentence. The math primer (Section 01.5) introduces one-way functions properly.

findings.quote: Spectre and Meltdown in Chapter 1. Buffer overflows in Chapter 3. Dirty COW in Chapter 4. BGP hijacking in Chapter 9. SYN floods in Chapter 10. DNS poisoning, TLS misissuance, XSS, CSRF, SQL injection.
findings.problem: Six clipped verbless fragments in a row, used for a staccato effect. The first five have chapter references and the last five attacks have none, though they come from Ch11, Ch12 and Ch13.
findings.fix: Attacks have run through this whole book: Spectre and Meltdown in Chapter 1, buffer overflows in Chapter 3, Dirty COW in Chapter 4, BGP hijacking in Chapter 9, SYN floods in Chapter 10, DNS poisoning and forged certificates in Chapter 11, XSS and CSRF in Chapter 12, SQL injection in Chapter 13. (The ledger's first clause 'Attacks have run through this whole book' stays.)

findings.quote: DNS poisoning, TLS misissuance, XSS, CSRF, SQL injection.
findings.problem: 'TLS misissuance' is insider shorthand that the book never uses or defines anywhere else. It is also wrong in detail: TLS is not issued. Certificates are mis-issued by a CA, which is the DigiNotar case in Ch11 and the 'fraudulent certificate' wording of ch14-tls-pqc-p4.
findings.fix: Say "forged certificates" (or "mis-issued certificates") in place of "TLS misissuance".

findings.quote: Diffie–Hellman 1976, the second invention of cryptography.
findings.problem: With no context, a newcomer reading the contents line cannot decode the metaphor, since cryptography already had two thousand years of history. A reader who knows Ch14's own GCHQ strip (Williamson found Diffie–Hellman in 1974) will read 'second invention' as 'invented second, after GCHQ', which is not what is meant.
findings.fix: Diffie–Hellman 1976: two strangers agree on a key in public.

findings.quote: [ch1-hero-lead] Before there was the internet, there was a mathematician who died before seeing what he built.
findings.problem: The only mathematician whose death Ch1 records is Turing (ch1-context-p11, 1954), and he did see machines built on his idea. The Manchester Baby ran in 1948. Turing joined the Manchester Computing Machine Laboratory that year and wrote the Programmers' Handbook for the Ferranti Mark 1 (1951). The Pilot ACE, built from his design, ran in 1950. 'Before there was the internet' also points at nothing: Ch1 never mentions the internet. A newcomer cannot decode the riddle, and an expert knows it is false.
findings.fix: Replace the first two sentences: "In 1936 a 24-year-old mathematician described, on paper, a machine that could follow any rules written for it; twelve years later one was running." Keep "This is the story of computer architecture, told in the order civilization needed it." This also removes the repeat of the part tagline's 'sand' opening (P1O-09). Sources: computer50.org (Manchester Mark 1); Bonhams lot 28322/46 (Turing's 1951 Programmers' Handbook).

findings.quote: [chBridge-hero-lead] Five small pieces of hardware are what separate a computer from a calculator.
findings.problem: This contradicts the book's own definition of a computer. Ch1 defines a computer by universality and the stored program (ch1-context-p5, ch1-vonneumann-p3), and it calls ENIAC 'the first general-purpose electronic computer' even though ENIAC had no privilege bit, MMU, trap table or timer. The 8086 that opens Ch3 had no privilege levels and no paging either, and it ran the IBM PC. The Bridge's own timer section (chBridge-timer-p1) describes a working CPU with no timer. What the five features separate is a machine where one program, the kernel, can own and share the hardware from one where it cannot. That is what the lead's third sentence says.
findings.fix: "Five small pieces of hardware let one program, the kernel, own a computer and share it safely among all the others: a privilege bit, a trap, a memory-management unit, a timer, and a way to reach devices." (This also fixes P1O-08.)

findings.quote: [ch1] Era covered 1936 → 1974
findings.problem: 1974 appears nowhere in Chapter 1; this label is the only place in part-1.html that has it. The chapter runs well past it: Moore's Law until about 2015 (ch1-transistor-p10), Spectre and Meltdown in 2018 (ch1-cpu-p11), and the Apple M4 of 2024, which carries a timeline entry and two figures (Figs 1.6, 1.7). It also starts before 1936, with Hilbert's 1928 question and the human computers of the nineteenth century. A reader who compares the label with the chapter's most vivid figures will stop.
findings.fix: "1936 → present", which matches Ch3 and the Bridge, or "1936 → 2024".

findings.quote: [ch2-hero-lead] He died before electricity was understood, never imagining a circuit.
findings.problem: Boole died in 1864. By then Ohm's law (1827), Faraday's induction (1831) and Kirchhoff's circuit laws (1845, two years before Boole's book) were all published, and telegraph circuits crossed continents. Electricity was well understood, and 'circuit' was an everyday word. The chapter's own claim is narrower and correct: he died 33 years before the electron was discovered and never saw electricity used in computing (ch2-boole-p5). The lead overstates it into a falsehood. A newcomer would come away believing electricity was unknown in the 1860s.
findings.fix: "He died in 1864, more than seventy years before anyone built his algebra out of switches." Source: Wikipedia, Kirchhoff's circuit laws (first described 1845); MacTutor, Kirchhoff biography.

findings.quote: [ch2-hero-lead] A century later, his algebra became the only mathematics that machines can do.
findings.problem: This is an aphorism closer that is false three ways. (1) Analog machines did calculus with no Boolean algebra at all: Bush's differential analyzer, which Shannon operated at MIT before writing his thesis, is one. (2) The chapter's own sections 04 to 06 teach machines doing arithmetic, two's complement and floating point. These are built from gates, but they are not 'only' Boolean algebra. (3) The section says logicians 'reshaped it into the Boolean algebra used today' (ch2-boole-p5), and the 2026-10-12 audit corrected the glossary for crediting Boole with the modern algebra, so 'his algebra' brings back that slip. Also, Shannon's 1937 thesis came 90 years after 1847, and Fig 2.2's caption says 'Ninety years apart'.
findings.fix: "Ninety years later, a reshaped form of it became the logic every digital circuit is built from."

findings.quote: [part opener] Before any program runs, a billion tiny switches must already agree on what "true" and "false" mean, and one program, the kernel, must already be standing watch.
findings.problem: The sentence contradicts itself: before any program runs, one program must already be running. It also contradicts Chapter 1, which teaches that in the 1950s each program had the whole machine to itself with no kernel (ch1-kernel-p1, Fig 1.13), and that the kernel was invented later. A careful reader stops on the first page of the Part. 'A billion' also understates the book's own figures: about fifteen billion in a phone (ch1-transistor-p10) and 28 billion in the M4.
findings.fix: "Before your program runs, billions of tiny switches must already agree on what "true" and "false" mean, and another program, the kernel, must already be standing watch."

findings.quote: [part opener, Bridge card] what the silicon must provide before any kernel can exist.
findings.problem: The Bridge itself says otherwise. chBridge-timer-p1 describes a cooperative kernel sharing a CPU that has no timer. Historically, UNIX was first written in 1969 (Ch1) for a PDP-7 with no memory protection, and its first PDP-11 port ran on an 11/20 with no memory management. What needs the five features is a kernel that can protect programs from each other and take the CPU back. Source: TUHS list (Wilson; Ritchie as quoted there); gunkies.org UNIX First Edition.
findings.fix: "what the silicon must provide before a kernel can keep programs apart and share the CPU among them."

findings.quote: [chBridge-hero-lead] A privilege bit. A trap. A page-table walker. A timer. A way to talk to the world. ... Part I cannot end without naming them.
findings.problem: This is a run of five clipped dramatic fragments, the pattern the brief bans, and it ends on an announcing sentence that does no job (law 2). 'A page-table walker' also names only part of the third feature: the section, the Topics line and the synthesis all call it the MMU, which includes the TLB and the permission check. A newcomer reaching the Bridge has not met the term.
findings.fix: Fold the list into one sentence, as in P1O-02's fix (privilege bit, trap, memory-management unit, timer, a way to reach devices). Keep "Together they are the conditions under which one program can be made to own the machine." and cut "Part I cannot end without naming them."

findings.quote: [part opener] Before software, there is sand. Before logic, there is voltage. Before any program runs ... / [ch1-hero-lead] Before there was software, there was sand.
findings.problem: The tagline is a three-part 'Before X, Y' anaphora, and the next text the reader sees, the Ch1 lead, repeats its first line almost word for word. The Ch1 and Ch2 leads then both turn on a man who 'died before'. The repeated shape across the three openings reads as a template, and the repeated sentence is a law-2 echo.
findings.fix: Keep the tagline's opening and start the Ch1 lead differently (P1O-01's fix does this). P1O-04's fix removes the 'died before' echo in Ch2.

findings.quote: [part opener] This is where the story has to begin: in the place most books skip.
findings.problem: This is an unsupported aphorism closer. Many standard introductions start from transistors and gates: Petzold's Code, Patt and Patel, Nand2Tetris, Bryant and O'Hallaron, and Tanenbaum's Structured Computer Organization, a title the book itself cites in UNDER.md §5.
findings.fix: "This is where the story has to begin."

findings.quote: [ch2] Era covered 1847 → 1985
findings.problem: The chapter's latest events come after 1985: the Patriot failure of 25 February 1991 (ch2-float-p11, Fig 2.12) and the Ariane 5 explosion of 1996 (ch2-twos-p10).

findings.quote: [ch3] Era covered 1949 → present
findings.problem: Nothing in Chapter 3 is dated 1949 or refers to it; this label is the only place in part-1.html that has the year. The chapter's earliest dates are C in 1972 (ch3-overflow-p8) and the 8086 in 1978, which opens the chapter (ch3-isa-p1). A reader cannot tell what 1949 refers to.
findings.fix: "1972 → present", or name the 1949 event (EDSAC's first assembler-style loader) somewhere in ch3-isa.

findings.quote: [chBridge] Era covered 1965 → present
findings.problem: The Bridge dates nothing, so 1965 points at nothing in the text. The five features also predate it. CTSS (1961–63) added a mode bit that trapped user I/O to the supervisor, memory protection and an interval timer to the IBM 7090/7094. The Atlas (1962) introduced paged virtual memory. Source: MIT CTSS RPQ documents (people.csail.mit.edu/saltzer/CTSS); gunkies.org CTSS.
findings.fix: "1961 → present" (CTSS) if the start is kept, or change the label to the present-day machines the Bridge describes (x86-64 and ARM).

findings.quote: [ch3-hero-lead] Below every Python script, every JavaScript framework, every neural network, there is a sequence of instructions written in the only language a processor truly understands.
findings.problem: This is a reflexive triplet ('every X, every Y, every Z') standing in for one plain claim, the pattern the brief bans.
findings.fix: "Below every program you run, however high-level, there is a sequence of instructions in the only language a processor understands: its own machine code."

findings.quote: [part opener cards] ...and IEEE 754. / ...Privilege rings, the trap mechanism, the MMU, the timer, MMIO, and DMA...
findings.problem: The Part's contents cards are the first thing a newcomer reads, and they use bare standard numbers and acronyms (IEEE 754, MMU, MMIO, DMA) that the chapters only explain later. The Ch2 card names the standard, while the Ch2 Topics line says 'Floats'.
findings.fix: Ch2: "...and how computers store fractions (IEEE 754)." Bridge: "Privilege rings, the trap mechanism, the memory-management unit, the timer, and the paths to devices (MMIO and DMA): ..."

findings.quote: [ch1] TopicsCPU · Memory · Kernel · OS / [Ch1 card] Transistors, Von Neumann's insight, the CPU, and why the kernel had to be invented.
findings.problem: The Topics line leaves out the chapter's first three sections: Turing's machine, the transistor (its longest section) and the stored-program architecture. 'Kernel' and 'OS' then name a single section twice. The contents card leaves out section 06, Memory, which the Topics line includes.
findings.fix: Topics: "Turing · Transistor · CPU · Kernel · Memory". Card: "Transistors, von Neumann's insight, the CPU, the memory hierarchy, and why the kernel had to be invented."

findings.quote: [Ch1 card] Transistors, Von Neumann's insight, the CPU,
findings.problem: 'Von' is capitalised in the middle of a sentence. The section prose writes 'John von Neumann' (ch1-vonneumann-p2). The capital is right only at the start of a heading or title, as in 'Von Neumann bottleneck' and Fig 1.8.
findings.fix: "Transistors, von Neumann's insight, the CPU, ..."

findings.quote: [End of Part I] The Substrate is built.
findings.problem: 'Substrate' is capitalised as if it were a proper name. The Part is titled 'The Physical World', the meta description and Part II's opener write 'the substrate' in lower case, and the matching Part III closer reads 'The network is built.'
findings.fix: "The substrate is built."

findings.quote: Control-Flow Integrity: a compiler-inserted runtime check that every indirect call or return lands on a target the compiler judged valid for that call site.
findings.problem: This brings back an error the ledger already corrected. UNDER.md §4g (Part IV law-4 row, 2026-10-15) changed ch15-memory-p3 from CFI checking "every indirect call and return" to indirect calls only, because shipped CFI (Clang CFI, MSVC CFG) checks forward edges and returns are guarded by shadow stacks and PAC. The section now says "Returns are guarded by the shadow stack and Pointer Authentication below." The tooltip still says CFI checks returns, so it disagrees with both the ledger and the section.
findings.fix: Control-Flow Integrity: a check the compiler inserts before every indirect call, making sure the target is one it recorded as valid for that call site. Returns are guarded separately, by shadow stacks and Pointer Authentication.

findings.quote: indentation marching across the screen and error handling impossible: the price of JavaScript's callback era.
findings.problem: The defining section (ch12-loop-p4) says error handling was "tedious", and Fig 12.4's strip says "every level needs its own error handling; forget one and the error is lost". Error handling in nested callbacks was possible, just repetitive and easy to get wrong, so "impossible" is false and contradicts the text it sits beside.
findings.fix: Code with three or four callbacks nested inside each other: the indentation marches across the screen and every level needs its own error handling. It was the price of JavaScript's callback era.

findings.quote: The property of relational algebra that every operation returns a relation, so any result can feed the next operation; it is what makes SQL composable.
findings.problem: book.js attaches this tooltip to every matching em/strong outside the defining section. That includes ch12-eich, where "(a closure)" means a JavaScript function that keeps access to the variables around it. A reader in Chapter 12, who has not reached Chapter 13 yet, who hovers or taps "closure" gets the relational-algebra meaning, which is wrong there.
findings.fix: In JavaScript (Chapter 12), a function that keeps access to the variables around it after the code that made them has finished. In relational algebra (Chapter 13), the property that every operation returns a relation, so any result can feed the next operation, which is what makes SQL composable.

findings.quote: A sequence of small, simple opcodes for a virtual machine, into which Python compiles source code before the interpreter executes it.
findings.problem: By Chapter 7 the book has defined "virtual machine" only one way (ch4-security-p9/p10): something that imitates a whole computer, guest kernel and all, on a hypervisor. The defining section says "an imaginary processor" instead. A newcomer reading this tooltip would picture a hypervisor VM running Python bytecode.
findings.fix: A sequence of small, simple instructions for an imaginary processor. Python compiles source code into them, and CPython's interpreter loop then reads and runs them one at a time.

findings.quote: Intel's hardware defence, centred on a shadow stack, against ROP and JOP
findings.problem: The book never explains JOP in its prose. It appears only as a label in kept-original Fig 15.2 ("JOP · 2011 · jump-oriented"), so the tooltip leans on jargon. The wording also implies the shadow stack stops JOP, but a shadow stack only protects returns. CET's separate indirect-branch tracking handles jump-oriented attacks, and the section does not mention it.
findings.fix: Control-flow Enforcement Technology: Intel's hardware defence against ROP, built around a shadow stack, a protected second copy of each return address that the CPU compares when the function returns. It has shipped in 11th-generation Core CPUs since 2020.

findings.quote: Vint Cerf, who with Bob Kahn published the 1974 paper that defined TCP/IP, the protocols ARPANET switched to in 1983.
findings.problem: The 1974 Cerf–Kahn paper described one protocol, the Transmission Control Program. TCP and IP were split into two only in 1978 (historyofinformation.com/detail.php?id=915; ICANN Turing Award release, 2005). The book itself is precise here: ch10-why-p1 says "Its protocol, which they called simply TCP", and Fig 9.x labels 1974 "the first TCP paper". So the tooltip disagrees with the book and overstates the history.
findings.fix: Vint Cerf, who with Bob Kahn published the 1974 paper that defined TCP. Split into TCP and IP in 1978, it became the protocol pair the ARPANET switched to in 1983.

findings.quote: A high-frequency sinusoid that a medium such as radio, DSL or cable can transport, onto which bits are imposed by modulation.
findings.problem: "Sinusoid" appears nowhere in the book. The defining section (ch8-encoding-p6) says "a steady high-frequency wave the medium carries well". A newcomer gets a technical word the text never uses, in place of the plain one it does use.
findings.fix: A steady high-frequency wave that a medium such as radio, DSL or cable carries well. Modulation changes its size, speed or phase in step with the bits.

findings.quote: The web is the layer above it: three protocols invented in 1989 at a particle physics lab
findings.problem: The line sits right under the title "HTTP · DNS · TLS", so a reader takes the three protocols to be HTTP, DNS and TLS. The chapter then says otherwise: DNS was designed by Mockapetris in 1983 (ch11-dns-p1) and TLS grew out of Netscape's SSL in 1994 to 1999 (ch11-tls-p1). Berners-Lee's own three (URL, HTTP, HTML; ch11-bernerslee-p4) are not all protocols. They also were not invented in 1989: that year brought only the proposal, and the first server ran at Christmas 1990 (ch11-bernerslee-p1, Fig 11.1 caption; the §4g Pass 16 row moved the server date to Christmas 1990). So the lead plants two wrong facts that the chapter later contradicts.
findings.fix: Name the parts and date them correctly, e.g. "The web is the layer above it: three conventions Tim Berners-Lee proposed at a particle physics lab in 1989 and built in 1990 (an address, a request, a page format), the older naming system DNS, and TLS, the encryption that rides beneath HTTPS."

findings.quote: plus a handful of cryptographic primitives invented in the 1970s by mathematicians
findings.problem: ch11-crypto-p1 names the three primitives TLS needs: hashing, symmetric encryption and public-key cryptography. The two the chapter names concretely are SHA-256 and AES, both NIST standards from 2001 (ch11-crypto-p4, p6), and its key exchange runs on elliptic curves (1985). Only public-key key agreement (Diffie–Hellman 1976, RSA 1977) dates from the 1970s.
findings.fix: "plus cryptography built on one 1970s idea, public-key key agreement", or drop the decade.

findings.quote: By the end of this chapter you will be able to read every byte of an HTTPS request from voltage to JSON.
findings.problem: The part opener makes the same promise for the end of Part III ("By the end you will be able to read every layer of an HTTPS request from voltage to JSON"), and ch12-security-p11 makes it a third time for after all five chapters. So the ch11 lead disagrees about when the reader gets there. "Every byte" of an HTTPS request is ciphertext; ch11-crypto-p1 says that is the whole point. JSON is never taught in Part III (ch11 has only a strip aside on JSON Merge Patch).
findings.fix: Keep the promise once, in the opener, as "every layer" ending at something the part teaches (e.g. "from voltage on copper to the page on screen"). Cut the sentence from the ch11 lead.

findings.quote: Brendan Eich was given ten working days, in May 1995, to design a scripting language for the Netscape browser.
findings.problem: Wirfs-Brock and Eich, "JavaScript: The First 20 Years" (HOPL IV, 2020, §2.2), say Eich "prototyped the first Mocha implementation in ten contiguous days in May, 1995", which he believes was May 6 to 15. May 6, 1995 was a Saturday and May 15 a Monday, so the span covers two weekends: they were not working days. The deadline was for "a feasibility demonstration", a prototype; the language went on changing until Navigator 2.0 shipped in March 1996. ch12-eich-p1 repeats "ten working days" (correct it in the same pass). Source: https://dokk.org/library/javascript_the_first_20_years_2020
findings.fix: "In May 1995 Brendan Eich had ten days to build a working prototype of a scripting language for the Netscape browser." Change ch12-eich-p1 to "ten days" to match.

findings.quote: Voltage to packets to TCP to HTTP to JavaScript. Five chapters, every layer from copper to pixels. Part IV turns to where information lives at rest: the relational database, real cryptography, and the unified security chapter that ties Parts I through III together.
findings.problem: Law 2. The paragraph just before it, ch12-security-p11, says the same things in the same order: Part III complete, voltage to packets to reliability to documents to JavaScript, then "Part IV turns to where information lives at rest", the relational database, the cryptography, and the security chapter tying Parts I to III together. The reader gets the same summary twice in a row.
findings.fix: Say it once. Since every part's closer carries this summary, cut ch12-security-p11 (or keep only its first sentence) and leave the closer as the single summary.

findings.quote: The voltage that flips a transistor inside a CPU is, at a different scale, the voltage that crosses a continent.
findings.problem: The chapter's own Fig 8.1 and its strip say a long-distance link carries light in glass, and that repeaters amplify the light "without turning it back into electricity". So no voltage crosses a continent, and a reader who has just learned that will stop here. The sentence also appears verbatim in the part opener and again in the ch8 hero lead, with a third variant as the ch8-bridge title, which breaks law 2.
findings.fix: Keep it once, made true, e.g. in the opener: "The bit that a voltage carries inside a CPU is the same bit that crosses a continent, as light in glass." Rewrite the ch8 lead's first sentence so it does not repeat the opener.

findings.quote: The phone company spent a century building a network where every call got its own dedicated wire.
findings.problem: From 1918 long-distance trunks carried several calls on one pair of wires (AT&T's Type A carrier, Pittsburgh–Baltimore, frequency-division multiplexing; later coaxial cable and T1 in 1962). What a call reserved was a circuit, a share of capacity held for the whole call, not a wire. That reservation of capacity is exactly the contrast the chapter draws (ch9-circuits-p2: "the capacity is yours alone"). Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carrier_telephony
findings.fix: "...a network where every call reserved its own circuit, a slice of capacity held from dial to hang-up."

findings.quote: turn a network of packets into a worldwide library of trustworthy documents
findings.problem: TLS proves which server you are talking to and protects the bytes in transit (ch11-tls-p2). It says nothing about whether a document is trustworthy. The phrase blurs authenticated with true.
findings.fix: "into a worldwide library of documents you can fetch by name and receive untampered".

findings.quote: Era covered 1989 → present
findings.problem: Two of the six sections teach older work: DNS, designed in 1983 (ch11-dns-p1), and Diffie–Hellman, 1976 (ch11-crypto-p7). The lead itself says "invented in the 1970s" a few lines above this range.
findings.fix: "Era covered 1976 → present" (or 1983 if the crypto is treated as background).

findings.quote: for a misconfigured router in Pakistan to take YouTube off the air for the whole world for two hours
findings.problem: The chapter's own account (Fig 9.11 desc and caption) is that Pakistan Telecom deliberately announced the /24 "to block YouTube inside Pakistan". The error was the leak, which its upstream PCCW passed on, and the hijack won "almost everywhere", not across the whole world. The lead's version contradicts the figure the reader meets in the same chapter.
findings.fix: "...for a block meant only for Pakistan to leak out and take YouTube offline almost everywhere for two hours."

findings.quote: the protocol that pretends a noisy network is reliable
findings.problem: Ch10 teaches that IP loses, reorders and duplicates packets, mostly because queues overflow under congestion (ch10-aimd). Noise is a link-layer problem, handled by Ch8's encodings and checksums. Right after Shannon, "noisy" points the newcomer at the wrong layer. TCP also does not pretend: it actually delivers reliably by resending.
findings.fix: "the protocol that makes a network that loses packets behave reliably".

findings.quote: the architectural decision to send packets rather than circuits
findings.problem: Circuits are reserved, not sent, so a newcomer who has not yet met circuit switching cannot parse the contrast.
findings.fix: "the decision to share the wires as packets rather than reserve a circuit for each conversation".

findings.quote: The mathematics of how much information any of them can carry. The encodings that turn ones and zeros into wave shapes. The local-network protocols that share the substrate. And the layer model that lets every conversation about networking refer back to a single picture.
findings.problem: Four verbless fragments in a row. The last one also overclaims ("every conversation") and says "the layer model" and "a single picture" when the chapter teaches two models, OSI and TCP/IP (section 06; the opener card says "layer models").
findings.fix: One sentence with a verb: "Then the mathematics of how much any of them can carry, the encodings that turn bits into signals, the protocols that let many machines share one medium, and the two layer models the rest of the book refers back to."

findings.quote: Its mathematics is control theory; its engineering is forty years of careful refinement; its attack surface is the reason every server has a SYN flood story.
findings.problem: A three-part parallel closer, and its third part overclaims ("every server"). "Forty years" undercounts: TCP dates from 1974, RFC 793 from 1981. §4g already replaced loose ages elsewhere (BGP "born in 1989").
findings.fix: "It finds its sending rate by feedback alone, it has been refined since 1974, and its handshake is the target of one of the oldest denial-of-service attacks, the SYN flood."

findings.quote: It is now the most widely deployed programming language in history.
findings.problem: Eich's own HOPL paper hedges this as "arguably the world's most broadly deployed". In the same lead, "the data language every modern database speaks" overclaims as well: relational databases speak SQL, and JSON is a column type or extension in many of them, not their language.
findings.fix: "It is arguably the most widely deployed programming language in history" and "Its object-literal syntax became JSON, the format most web services now exchange data in."

findings.quote: Reliability built on top of unreliable.
findings.problem: The noun is missing: "unreliable" is an adjective with nothing to modify.
findings.fix: "Reliability built on top of an unreliable network."

findings.quote: copper, fiber, radio
findings.problem: The opener's Ch8 card and the ch8 hero lead spell "fiber". Everywhere else the book uses "fibre" (16 times in Part III, twice in Part V).
findings.fix: "copper, fibre, radio" in both places.

findings.quote: Packets: How The Internet Decided to Work
findings.problem: "The" is capitalised mid-title in the ch9 hero heading. The opener card reads "How the Internet" and the other hero titles keep small words lower case ("Problem of").
findings.fix:
"Packets: How
the Internet
Decided to Work".

findings.quote: Part IV turns to where information lives at rest: the relational database, real cryptography, and the unified security chapter
findings.problem: "Real cryptography" implies Ch11's cryptography was fake rather than a briefing. The colon also files cryptography and attack-and-defence under "where information lives at rest", which fits only the database chapter. ch12-security-p11 adds "and how it stays trustworthy" to cover them; the closer drops it.
findings.fix: "Part IV turns to where information lives at rest and how it is kept safe: the relational database, cryptography in mathematical depth, and the security chapter that ties Parts I to III together."

findings.quote: The elliptic-curve signature scheme published in 2011 by Daniel J. Bernstein and collaborators, used by TLS 1.3, SSH, Signal and WireGuard.
findings.problem: WireGuard uses no signature scheme. Its protocol page lists ChaCha20-Poly1305, Curve25519 for ECDH, BLAKE2s, SipHash24 and HKDF, with no Ed25519 (wireguard.com/protocol). Section ch14-ecc-p4 credits the pair 'Curve25519 and Ed25519' to the four systems together, and that is right. The glossary hands all four to Ed25519 alone, so a reader who knows WireGuard would stop here.
findings.fix: The elliptic-curve signature scheme published in 2011 by Daniel J. Bernstein and collaborators, built on the same curve as Curve25519. SSH and TLS 1.3 use it to sign; WireGuard uses the curve only for key exchange.

findings.quote: The largest hacker conference in the world, held every August in Las Vegas.
findings.problem: Not every year. DEF CON 25 ran 27 to 30 July 2017 at Caesars Palace (defcon.org DC 25 archive), and DEF CON 20 also ran in late July (2012). The DEF CON FAQ calls the slot late July or early August.
findings.fix: The largest hacker conference in the world, held in Las Vegas every summer, in late July or early August.

findings.quote: whose spare electrons or vacancies (holes) give the crystal mobile carriers, so a small voltage can switch it.
findings.problem: 'Mobile carriers' is a term the section never uses or explains; it speaks only of free electrons and holes. The definition also says doping by itself makes silicon switchable. Section ch1-transistor-p7 shows the switch comes from where n-type and p-type silicon meet, which leaves a barrier that the gate voltage opens.
findings.fix: Salting pure silicon with a trace of another element. An atom with an extra outer electron leaves electrons free to move (n-type); one with one fewer leaves gaps called holes (p-type). Where the two kinds meet, a small voltage can open or close the path.

findings.quote: by page JavaScript that writes URL parameters into the DOM unsafely.
findings.problem: The section avoids the term 'URL parameters' and says 'the part of the URL after the ?'. Fig 12.9's DOM-based example reads location.hash, the part after #, which is not a URL parameter and never reaches the server. That is the whole point of this variant, and the definition leaves it out.
findings.fix: Cross-site scripting carried out entirely in the browser: the page's own JavaScript copies part of the URL (after the ? or the #) into the page as HTML, so the script runs without the server ever echoing it.

findings.quote: a giant switch statement that reads each bytecode and dispatches it to the C handler
findings.problem: Pass 28 took the 'giant switch' wording out of Fig 7.6 (§4g Fig 7.6 row: the old caption was dated). The figure's strip now says ceval.c 'jumps from each instruction to its C handler, using computed gotos where the compiler supports them'. The glossary brings back the old picture. CPython builds use computed gotos where the compiler supports them, and 3.14 also has a tail-call build, so a plain switch is only the fallback.
findings.fix: CPython's bytecode loop (ceval.c): it reads each bytecode instruction in turn and jumps to the C code that carries it out, one case per instruction.

findings.quote: "section": "ch14-primer"
findings.problem: The glossary index sends the reader to ch14-primer, but that section names only the protocol Diffie–Hellman, never the person. Whitfield Diffie, the 1976 paper 'New Directions in Cryptography' and the 2015 Turing Award all appear in ch14-history, the section just before it. The definition itself is correct.
findings.fix: Keep the definition as it is, and anchor the entry at ch14-history, where Diffie and Hellman's 1976 paper and their 2015 Turing Award are told.

findings.quote: A kernel-managed counter, incremented and decremented atomically, that processes use as a gate to a shared resource; Edsger Dijkstra formalised the idea in 1965.
findings.problem: Calling it a kernel-managed counter brings back an error the fact ledger already corrected.
