The §4g Fig 4.18 row replaced 'sem_wait()/sem_post() are atomic in the kernel' with: on Linux the uncontended path is an atomic instruction in user space, and the kernel (futex) is entered only to sleep or wake. The defining section's own Fig 4.18 strip says so: 'atomic instructions on a counter in shared memory; the kernel is called only when someone must sleep or be woken.' The tooltip contradicts the figure beside it. (The ch4-ipc table row 'A kernel-managed counter' has the same wording.)
findings.fix: A counter, changed atomically, that processes use as a gate to a shared resource: entering takes one, or sleeps while it is 0, and leaving gives one back. The idea is Edsger Dijkstra's, from 1965; on Linux the counter sits in shared memory and the kernel is called only to put a process to sleep or wake it.

findings.quote: published RSA in 1977, the first practical public-key system.
findings.problem: The defining section (ch14-publickey) and ch14-history both present Diffie–Hellman, 1976, as the first public-key method, and it is practical: TLS 1.3 uses it on every connection. The glossary's own 'diffie hellman' entry dates it 1976. Calling RSA (1977) 'the first practical public-key system' contradicts the page the reader just read. What RSA was first at, in the open literature, is a public-key system that can both encrypt and sign. (The 'adleman' entry, not in this batch, has the same clause.)
findings.fix: Ron Rivest, who with Adi Shamir and Leonard Adleman at MIT published RSA in 1977, the first public-key system that could both encrypt and sign.

findings.quote: published RSA in 1977, the first practical public-key system.
findings.problem: Same clause as 'rivest'. Diffie–Hellman, which the book presents a year earlier (1976) and which TLS 1.3 runs on every connection, is a practical public-key system that predates RSA. So 'first practical public-key system' contradicts ch14-publickey and ch14-history.
findings.fix: Adi Shamir, who with Ron Rivest and Leonard Adleman at MIT published RSA in 1977, the first public-key system that could both encrypt and sign.

findings.quote: with a 256-bit output computed through 64 rounds of a Merkle–Damgård compression function.
findings.problem: The entry is defined in ch14-primer (01.5), which comes before ch14-hashing (02). The primer never mentions rounds, compression functions or Merkle–Damgård, so a reader at that point meets three unexplained terms in the tooltip. The phrase is also muddled. Merkle–Damgård is the construction that chains the compression function over 512-bit blocks; the 64 rounds happen inside the compression function for each block. ch14-hashing-p3 states it correctly.
findings.fix: The standard cryptographic hash function today: it turns any input into a 256-bit fingerprint quickly, and no practical way is known to run it backward or to find two inputs with the same fingerprint.

findings.quote: its ideas (closures, first-class functions) lie under JavaScript's C-like syntax.
findings.problem: The term 'first-class functions' appears nowhere in the book. ch12-eich-p2 explains the idea in plain words ('a function was a value that could be stored and passed around like a number') but never names it, so the tooltip uses jargon the reader has not been given.
findings.fix: A Lisp dialect; Brendan Eich was recruited to Netscape to bring it to the browser, and its ideas (functions as values that can be stored and passed around, closures) lie under JavaScript's C-like syntax.

findings.quote: The 2017 Google attack that produced two different PDF files with identical SHA-1 hashes
findings.problem: SHAttered was a joint result of CWI Amsterdam (Marc Stevens and others) and Google, announced together on 23 February 2017 (securityweek.com/first-sha-1-collision-attack-conducted-google-cwi; helpnetsecurity.com/2017/02/24/sha-1-collision-attack). Calling it 'the Google attack' drops the co-authors, the same kind of attribution slip §4g's Tier 2 corrected elsewhere. The 2^63 cost is right (2^63.1 SHA-1 computations).
findings.fix: The 2017 attack by CWI Amsterdam and Google that produced two different PDF files with identical SHA-1 hashes, at a cost of about 2⁶³ hash computations, breaking SHA-1's collision resistance.

findings.quote: FLP shows it cannot be guaranteed alongside liveness in an asynchronous system with even one crash.
findings.problem: The entry drops the qualifier 'deterministic'. The defining section keeps it ('no deterministic consensus protocol can guarantee both'), and so does the paired 'liveness' entry ('no deterministic consensus protocol can promise it alongside safety'). The section's own list of escapes includes randomness (Ben-Or). As written, the theorem reads broader than it is, and the two companion tooltips disagree.
findings.fix: The guarantee that a protocol never reaches an inconsistent decision; FLP shows that no deterministic consensus protocol can promise it alongside liveness in an asynchronous system with even one crash.

findings.quote: while Alan Kay's group worked on the Alto personal computer
findings.problem: The defining section (ch8-ethernet-p3) credits the Alto to Chuck Thacker and Butler Lampson. Commit f01c84e made exactly that correction, replacing "Alan Kay's group was inventing the personal computer (the Alto...)". The glossary still has the old attribution, so the tooltip contradicts the corrected prose beside it. The same text is also in the separate 'xerox parc' entry. The definition never says what PARC stands for either.
findings.fix: Xerox's Palo Alto Research Center, the lab where in 1973 Bob Metcalfe invented Ethernet, Chuck Thacker and Butler Lampson built the Alto personal computer, and Gary Starkweather had brought the laser printer to life.

findings.quote: Codd's name for pre-relational databases such as IMS and CODASYL
findings.problem: Two errors. (1) It calls CODASYL a database. The fact ledger corrected this ('ch13-codd-p2 CODASYL was a committee, not a database'), and the section itself calls CODASYL 'the network-model standard drawn up by committee'. (2) 'Navigational' was not Codd's name. His 1970 paper talks about access-path, ordering and indexing dependence. The term was made popular by Charles Bachman's 1973 Turing Award lecture 'The Programmer as Navigator' (Wikipedia, Navigational database). Note that ch13-codd-p1 ('Codd called the existing approach navigational') has the same attribution.
findings.fix: The name, made popular by Charles Bachman's 1973 lecture 'The Programmer as Navigator', for pre-relational databases such as IBM's IMS and those built to the CODASYL standard, whose programs walked pointer to pointer through tree- or network-shaped data.

findings.quote: every primitive in modern cryptography is built on one
findings.problem: The defining sentence (ch14-primer-p1) says 'Every primitive in this chapter except AES ... is built on a different one-way function'. The tooltip drops the exception and widens the claim to all of modern cryptography, so it contradicts the passage it comes from. It also drops the section's warning that one-way functions are assumed, not proven.
findings.fix: A computation that is easy to run forward and infeasible to run backward. Hashing, Diffie–Hellman, RSA, elliptic curves and the lattice schemes each rest on one (AES does not), though nobody has proved that any truly exists.

findings.quote: raises when a virtual page has no valid mapping
findings.problem: This leaves out the permission case. A write to a read-only page faults even though its mapping is valid. The same section depends on that case: copy-on-write fork, one of its 'two beautiful uses of page faults', and the invalid fault 'writing to a read-only page'. Fig BR.4 shows the same thing. A reader who has just read about copy-on-write will find that the tooltip excludes it.
findings.fix: The hardware exception the MMU raises when an access cannot go ahead: the page is not in RAM, or the access breaks its permissions, such as a write to a read-only page. The kernel's handler then maps the page, reads it from disk, copies it, or sends the process SIGSEGV.

findings.quote: rewriting addresses at a translation layer so many machines share one public IPv4 address
findings.problem: It explains 'translation' with 'a translation layer', which is a phrase the book never uses. It also leaves out the mechanism the section teaches (Fig 9.8): each outgoing connection gets its own port in a translation table, and that table is what lets many machines share one address.
findings.fix: Network Address Translation: a router rewrites each outgoing packet's private address to its own public one, gives the connection its own port and notes the pair in a table so replies find their way back, which lets many machines share one public IPv4 address. CGNAT is the same done by an ISP for thousands of homes.

findings.quote: on which the cryptography of Chapter 14, and so TLS, rests; one of the primitives that outlast every substrate
findings.problem: It claims too much. Chapter 14 itself rests AES and hashing on other ground, and moves TLS toward lattices. The section says the mathematical primitives 'almost always survive', not that they outlast every substrate. In Chapter 14 'primitive' also means a cryptographic building block, so the word is ambiguous here.
findings.fix: The mathematics of the whole numbers (primes, remainders, modular arithmetic), on which RSA, Diffie–Hellman and the elliptic curves of Chapter 14 rest; one of the mathematical ideas that survive changes of hardware because they do not depend on it.

findings.quote: as in cat server.log | grep "^ERROR" | sort | wc -l
findings.problem: The section's example is cat server.log | grep "^ERROR" | sort | uniq | wc -l. With uniq dropped, sort no longer does anything (sorting does not change a line count), so a careful reader stops and wonders why it is there.
findings.fix: A shell chain of processes joined by pipes, each reading standard input and writing standard output, as in cat server.log | grep "^ERROR" | sort | uniq | wc -l.

findings.quote: p + 1 advances by sizeof(int), four bytes on most systems
findings.problem: sizeof is a C operator the book never introduces (it does not appear anywhere in Part II). The section says the same thing in plain words: 'an int takes four bytes'.
findings.fix: Adding to a pointer counts in elements of the type it points at, not in bytes: if p is an int *, p + 1 is the address of the next int, four bytes further on most systems.

findings.quote: The one instruction (SYSCALL on x86-64, SVC on ARM, ECALL on RISC-V) that a user program executes to ask the kernel to do something on its behalf.
findings.problem: This says the system call is the instruction. The defining section (chBridge-trap-p1) says the program makes a system call, a request across the boundary, by executing one special instruction: the request is the system call and the instruction is only how it crosses. 'The one instruction' is also wrong by the book's own account: chBridge-trap-p4 and p6 say older Linux programs made system calls with int 0x80 (vector 128).
findings.fix: A user program's request for the kernel to do something on its behalf, such as reading a file. The program makes it by executing its chip's system-call instruction (SYSCALL on x86-64, SVC on ARM, ECALL on RISC-V), which traps into the kernel.

findings.quote: the cost class of the best known factoring algorithms, still hard in the cryptographic sense.
findings.problem: The defining paragraph (ch14-primer-p6) says 'Hard, in the cryptographic sense, means exponential' and calls factoring 'kinder'. The tooltip next to that paragraph says sub-exponential is 'still hard in the cryptographic sense', so the two contradict each other on the same screen. The rest of the entry is correct: the number field sieve is slower than exponential and faster than any polynomial.
findings.fix: Growth slower than exponential but faster than any polynomial. It is the cost of the best known factoring algorithms: gentler than a true exponential, which is why RSA keys need thousands of bits, but still far out of reach at those sizes.

findings.quote: Transmission Control Protocol: Cerf and Kahn's 1974 design for a reliable, ordered byte stream over IP's unreliable packets
findings.problem: This is anachronistic. In 1974 there was no separate IP. Cerf and Kahn's 1974 protocol (then the Transmission Control Program) did both jobs, and IP was split out of it in 1978 by Cerf, Postel and Cohen, with TCP version 4 (history of the split: elists.isoc.org/pipermail/internet-history/2022-June/008088.html; historyofcomputercommunications.info/section/8.11/TCP-to-TCP-IP-1976-1979/). As written, the entry says the 1974 design ran over IP.
findings.fix: Transmission Control Protocol: the reliable, ordered byte stream that runs over IP's unreliable packets. Cerf and Kahn first published it in 1974 (IP was split off from it in 1978), and congestion control was added later.

findings.quote: after the k-th consecutive collision each station waits a random number of slot-times between 0 and 2ᵏ − 1, so waits grow with congestion.
findings.problem: The entry never explains the word that makes the term 'truncated'. The defining strip (ch8-ethernet, Fig 8.8) says k stops growing at 10 and a station gives up after 16 tries; the §4g Fig 8.8 row records that cap as the correction. A reader cannot learn from this tooltip what is truncated.
findings.fix: Ethernet's collision rule: after the k-th collision in a row, a station waits a random 0 to 2ᵏ − 1 slot times. k stops growing at 10 (the truncation) and the station gives up after 16 tries, so the waits spread out as the line gets busier.

findings.quote: so the server holds state for half-open connections that never complete until its table fills.
findings.problem: Without a comma, 'never complete until its table fills' reads as if the connections complete once the table fills. The entry also stops before the harm, which is legitimate clients being refused (ch10-attacks-p2).
findings.fix: An attack that sends a stream of SYNs, often from spoofed addresses, so the server holds state for half-open connections that never complete, until its table fills and real clients are refused.

findings.quote: the small associative cache in the MMU
findings.problem: 'Associative' is cache-design jargon that the book never explains, and the defining section (chBridge-mmu-p5) does not use it. A newcomer gets nothing from the word.
findings.fix: Translation lookaside buffer: the small cache in the MMU that remembers recent virtual-to-physical translations, so the page-table walk runs only on a miss.

findings.quote: now carrying DSCP and ECN.
findings.problem: DSCP and ECN are bare acronyms that the book never expands or explains, either here or in ch9-ip's strip, so the second half of the definition tells a newcomer nothing.
findings.fix: Type of Service: an IPv4 header field once meant for priority hints, now split between a traffic-class marking (DSCP) and a congestion signal (ECN).

findings.quote: the book credits him with RAII.
findings.problem: The tooltip appears from ch6-stroustrup (Section 02) on, but RAII is first explained in Section 04, so here it is an unexplained acronym. 'The book credits him' is also a meta aside that is out of the book's voice. Stroustrup coined the term, and the book's own claim (ch6 Section 04) is that RAII was his most original contribution.
findings.fix: Bjarne Stroustrup, who arrived at Bell Labs in 1979 and grafted Simula's classes onto C to create C++. He also named RAII, the C++ rule that ties each resource to an object that gives it back automatically.

findings.quote: HTTP run over TLS, so every byte between browser and server is encrypted and the server's identity is proven by its certificate.
findings.problem: Says more than is true, and more than the book's own TLS section says. The ch11-tls strip states 'Only the two hellos cross in the clear'. The ClientHello also carries the site's name in clear (SNI), and IP and TCP headers are never encrypted. A reader would think an onlooker cannot see which site they visit. The second half also contradicts the book: the certificate only binds a public key to a name. The ch11-tls strip says the signature over the handshake is what proves the server holds the matching private key, since anyone can replay a public certificate.
findings.fix: HTTP carried inside a TLS connection: after the opening hellos, every request and page crosses the wire encrypted, and the server proves who it is with its certificate and a signature only its private key can make.

findings.quote: IP's control-message companion (protocol number 1), used for example when a router reports that a packet's TTL reached zero.
findings.problem: The defining section is ch8-layers, where ICMP is only a name in the layer-examples strip ('3: IP, ICMP'), and that strip is the only place the book uses the term. TTL and the header's protocol field are first taught in ch9-ip, so a reader at this point meets two terms nobody has explained.
findings.fix: Internet Control Message Protocol: IP's companion for reports about delivery rather than data, for example a router telling the sender that it had to drop a packet.

findings.quote: the body that chooses the operator of each DNS top-level domain, such as VeriSign for .com, and one of the root's operators.
findings.problem: 'Chooses the operator of each' top-level domain is wrong for country codes. ICANN signs contracts with the operators of generic domains like .com. Country-code domains are run by national registries chosen in their own countries (the defining section itself says 'fi by Traficom'), and ICANN's IANA function only records the delegation. 'One of the root's operators' is correct: ICANN runs L-root.
findings.fix: The Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers: the body that coordinates the DNS root, contracts the operators of generic top-level domains such as VeriSign for .com, and runs one of the root servers itself.

findings.quote: work of O(2^n) doubles with every extra bit of input, which is what makes a cryptographic problem hard.
findings.problem: The defining paragraph (ch14-primer-p6) adds a caveat right away: factoring, the problem under RSA, is only sub-exponential and is still hard because its cost outgrows any power of n. That wording is the fact ledger's Pass 29 correction. The tooltip presents exponential growth as the thing that makes crypto hard and drops the caveat, so it reads as if RSA rested on exponential work.
findings.fix: Growth that multiplies by a fixed factor at each step: work of O(2^n) doubles with every extra bit of input. Factoring, under RSA, grows more slowly (sub-exponential) but still faster than any power of n, which is enough to make it hard.

findings.quote: Horizontal escalation
findings.problem: The term is stored capitalised because it was extracted from the start of a sentence (ch4-security-p4 opens with it in bold). The tooltip header and the glossary index show 'Horizontal escalation' next to lower-case common nouns such as 'half adder' and 'hard link'. The definition itself is fine. The same extractor artefact affects other entries outside this batch: Vertical escalation, Circuit switching, Collision resistance, Connection migration, Partition tolerance, Speculative execution.
findings.fix: Store the term as 'horizontal escalation' and keep the definition: A privilege escalation that moves sideways, at the same privilege level, into another process's or user's data.

findings.quote: Multi-version concurrency control: writers append new row versions stamped with a transaction id and each reader sees a snapshot, so readers and writers never block each other.
findings.problem: This brings back an error the ledger already corrected. §4g (Part IV, law 4, 2026-10-15) changed ch13-acid-p8's claim that MVCC writers never overwrite a row in place, because InnoDB and Oracle update the row in place and keep the old version in an undo log. The section now says only PostgreSQL appends, while InnoDB updates in place with an undo log. The tooltip still says all writers append. The glossary entry comes from scripts/glossary-defs.json and was never updated.
findings.fix: Multi-version concurrency control: a writer never destroys a row version a reader may still need (PostgreSQL appends a new version, InnoDB keeps the old one in an undo log), and each reader sees a snapshot, so readers and writers never block each other.

findings.quote: has slowed to a near-halt below 3 nanometres, where transistors are a few atoms wide.
findings.problem: This is stale. Commit 7dba59b (Law 4, Chapter 18, 'Moore's law ... claims stated exactly') rewrote ch18-future-p1 from 'slowed to a near-halt below 3 nanometres because we are running into single-atom-width physics' to 'slowed sharply: the finest parts of a transistor are now only a few nanometres across, a few dozen atoms'. The glossary entry in scripts/glossary-defs.json still has the old claim, so the glossary contradicts the corrected sentence on both points: 'near-halt' against 'slowed sharply', and 'a few atoms' against 'a few dozen atoms'. 'A few atoms wide' is also wrong as a fact. A side issue: the key is a claim, not a term (a term-cue artefact); 'Moore's Law' would be the natural entry.
findings.fix: Moore's Law, the doubling of transistor density roughly every two years, has slowed sharply: a transistor's finest parts are now a few nanometres across, a few dozen atoms, and each further shrink leaks more current and costs more.

findings.quote: TLS reduces it to denial of service.
findings.problem: The defining section (ch14-tls-pqc, Fig 14.12's strip) uses MITM for DigiNotar's false *.google.com certificate, which was used for weeks to intercept Gmail users in Iran: a MITM that worked against TLS. The definition says flatly that TLS leaves only denial of service, so it contradicts the very example it explains. TLS protects only while every trusted CA behaves, which is the gap Certificate Transparency was built to close in the same section.
findings.fix: Man-in-the-middle: an attack in which an adversary between two parties relays their traffic while reading or rewriting it. TLS stops it as long as no trusted CA has issued the attacker a false certificate, as the breached DigiNotar did in 2011.

findings.quote: leaving the source valid but empty.
findings.problem: Stated as a rule for all objects, this is wrong. The C++ standard leaves moved-from library objects 'in a valid but unspecified state'. Empty is true of the book's vector example (Fig 6.8), not in general. The book itself says so later in Chapter 6 ('Use-after-move: a moved-from object is in a valid but unspecified state'), so the tooltip contradicts the text and invites the very bug that passage warns about.
findings.fix: The C++11 mechanism that lets one object take over another's internal buffers instead of copying them; the source stays valid but its value is unspecified (a moved-from vector is empty), so it should not be relied on afterwards.

findings.quote: expired timers and DOM events
findings.problem: The DOM is first explained in ch12-dom, two sections after ch12-loop defines this term, so 'DOM' is an unexplained acronym for a reader who has reached the defining section. The section itself says 'clicks and other page events'.
findings.fix: The queue, also called the callback queue, of JavaScript callbacks ready to run from completed I/O, expired timers, and clicks and other page events; the event loop takes one per turn.

findings.quote: The second phase of Raft:
findings.problem: Raft has no numbered phases. Its authors split it into subproblems (leader election, log replication, safety), and log replication is the normal work a leader does once elected, not a step in each decision. The same section has just said 'Paxos works in two-phase rounds', so 'second phase' invites the reader to map it onto Paxos's phase 2. Also, 'a majority acknowledge' leaves out the leader's own copy, which Fig 17.5 counts (A, B, C: 3 of 5).
findings.fix: Raft's normal work once a leader is elected: the leader appends each client command to its log, copies it to the other nodes, and commits the entry once a majority of the cluster holds it.

findings.quote: anything larger must be fragmented.
findings.problem: Not true in general, and it pulls against the defining section, which says fragmentation is generally avoided and IPv6 forbids routers to fragment. An IPv6 packet, or an IPv4 packet marked don't-fragment, that is too big for a link is dropped and the sender is told to send smaller packets (path MTU discovery, Fig 9.5's strip).
findings.fix: Maximum transmission unit: the largest packet a link can carry in one piece (1500 bytes on standard Ethernet); a larger packet must be split into fragments or is dropped, and IPv6 routers never split one.

findings.quote: raises a page fault when something is wrong.
findings.problem: A page fault also fires when a page is simply not in RAM yet. Fig BR.4's check includes 'present', and Chapter 4 (ch4-vm-p9) says outright that most page faults are not errors. Shown as a tooltip in Part II and later, 'when something is wrong' contradicts that.
findings.fix: Memory management unit: the circuit between the CPU and RAM that translates every virtual address to a physical one, checks permissions, and raises a page fault when the page is not in memory or the access is not allowed.

findings.quote: runs drivers and filesystems as user-space processes.
findings.problem: 'User space' is used nowhere in Part I and appears only later in Chapter 4. The defining section (ch4-anatomy-p5) says 'separate programs in Ring 3', which the reader already has from Chapter 1 and the Bridge.
findings.fix: A kernel that keeps only the minimum in Ring 0 (message passing, basic memory protection, minimal scheduling) and runs drivers and filesystems as separate programs in Ring 3.

findings.quote: produced by dividing by zero or overflowing the largest representable number
findings.problem: Dividing zero by zero gives NaN, not infinity. The defining section (ch2-float-p9) says "a non-zero number is divided by zero", and the NaN entry gives 0.0 / 0.0 as its example, so this tooltip contradicts both.
findings.fix: The IEEE 754 special value with an all-ones exponent and a zero mantissa, produced when a non-zero number is divided by zero or a result grows past the largest double; the sign bit gives its direction.

findings.quote: writing every change first to a journal, then to its real place
findings.problem: This brings back the error §4g corrected in the Fig 4.13 row ("does every write twice"). By default ext4 (data=ordered) and NTFS log only metadata, and file contents go through the journal only in full data journaling (ext4 data=journal), as ch4-fs's own strip says. The entry's home is also wrong: ch4-security only names the word in the Ch4 summary, and journaling is taught in ch4-fs.
findings.fix: Of a filesystem: logging each change to its structure (inodes, free lists, directories) in a journal, sealed by a commit record, before applying it, so after a crash the kernel replays or discards whole changes in seconds instead of scanning the disk. (Home section: ch4-fs.)

findings.quote: Building one class on another; in memory, one struct embedded inside another.
findings.problem: The home is ch7-vanrossum, where the only use is Fig 7.2's strip label "The inheritance. From ABC, Python took indentation...", meaning heritage, not class inheritance. The object-oriented idea is taught in ch6-classes ("a Circle object begins with a complete Shape"), so the glossary index sends the reader to a Python history paragraph that never explains the term.
findings.fix: Building one class on another, so the new class starts with everything the old one has; in memory a Circle object begins with a complete Shape, one struct embedded inside another. (Home section: ch6-classes.)

findings.quote: FLP shows that no deterministic consensus protocol can promise it alongside safety under pure asynchrony
findings.problem: The entry leaves out the condition the theorem needs: that even one process may crash. Asynchrony on its own does not rule out consensus. The paired 'safety' entry and ch17-consensus-p8/p11 both state the crash condition, so this tooltip misstates FLP.
findings.fix: The guarantee that a protocol always eventually reaches a decision; FLP shows that in a fully asynchronous system where even one machine may crash, no deterministic consensus protocol can promise it alongside safety.

findings.quote: Argo CD and Flux run it as a loop, while Terraform and Pulumi run it only when a person asks, working out the changes needed (the plan) and applying them once. Argo CD and Flux run it as a loop, Terraform and Pulumi as a plan applied on demand.
findings.problem: Found while reading the k8s packet: the paragraph says the same thing twice in a row in public/part-5.html (around line 1690). It is a leftover from an edit, and the reader trips over it. It breaks law 2.
findings.fix: Delete the second sentence ("Argo CD and Flux run it as a loop, Terraform and Pulumi as a plan applied on demand.") and keep the first.

findings.quote: where a filesystem writes each intended change before applying it
findings.problem: "Each intended change" suggests that file contents are journaled too. That is the claim §4g corrected in the Fig 4.13 row: by default ext4 and NTFS journal only metadata, as the ch4-fs strip says.
findings.fix: A small, dedicated disk region where a filesystem first logs each change to its structure (inodes, free lists, directories, and file contents only in modes such as ext4's data=journal), so after a crash it replays the committed changes instead of scanning the whole disk.

findings.quote: the body whose RFCs standardise internet protocols, from QUIC in 2021 to the catalogue of BGP route-leak types in RFC 7908
findings.problem: The book never expands or explains "RFC": there is no glossary entry and no gloss in Part III, so the definition rests on an unexplained term. Its second example is also wrong: RFC 7908 (June 2016) is an Informational RFC that classifies route leaks. It is not a standard (rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7908).
findings.fix: The Internet Engineering Task Force: the open body that standardises internet protocols, publishing them as numbered documents called RFCs (Requests for Comments), such as RFC 9000, which made QUIC a standard in 2021.

findings.quote: published the 1974 paper that defined TCP/IP
findings.problem: The 1974 Cerf–Kahn paper described one protocol, the Transmission Control Program. IP was split out of it in 1978. The defining section (ch10-why-p1) gets this right: "Its protocol, which they called simply TCP". Calling it TCP/IP is anachronistic.
findings.fix: Bob Kahn, who with Vint Cerf published the 1974 paper that defined TCP, the single protocol later split into TCP and IP.

findings.quote: Codd's principle that queries describe the result wanted, not the procedure
findings.problem: The definition never says what the queries are independent of. Codd's 1970 principle is data independence: programs and users are unaffected by how, and whether, the stored representation changes, which is exactly what the owner's pull-quote above it says. Defining it only as declarative querying drops the meaning the name carries.
findings.fix: Codd's principle that programs and queries must not depend on how the data is stored: a query describes the result wanted, not the procedure, so the engine may change the storage or choose any strategy that gives the same answer.

findings.quote: A type 1 (bare-metal) hypervisor, like ESXi, Xen and Hyper-V, of the kind every public cloud uses.
findings.problem: The entry gives KVM's category but never says what KVM is: no expansion, and nothing that sets it apart from the three products it lists. A newcomer comes away knowing only that it is "one of those". Other entries in this batch (IDS, IDT, IHL) expand their acronyms.
findings.fix: Kernel-based Virtual Machine: the hypervisor built into the Linux kernel, which turns Linux itself into a type 1 hypervisor like ESXi, Xen and Hyper-V; AWS's Nitro hypervisor is built from it.

findings.quote: the source field is set by the sender and verified nowhere along the path
findings.problem: Read alone, the tooltip says nothing ever checks the source. The defining section (ch9-security-p1) goes on to say most ISPs filter forged sources at their edge (BCP 38), and Fig 9.10 shows the edge router dropping exactly such a packet.
findings.fix: Writing a false source address into a packet's IP header, possible because the sender fills in the source field and routers forward on the destination alone; only networks that filter at their edge (BCP 38) stop it.

findings.quote: "section": "ch12-eich"
findings.problem: The home section only mentions "IEEE 754 doubles" and points back to "Chapter 2.6". The standard is taught in ch2-float ("## IEEE 754: the universal floating-point standard"), so the glossary index sends the reader to a section that does not explain it. The definition text itself is correct.
findings.fix: Keep the text and move the home to ch2-float: "The floating-point standard, published by the IEEE in 1985, that defines how processors represent fractional numbers; every JavaScript number is a 64-bit IEEE 754 double."

findings.quote: The first phase of Raft: nodes wait out randomised timeouts, and the first to expire starts a new term
findings.problem: The entry leaves out what starts an election, which the defining figure stresses: no heartbeat arrives from a leader (Fig 17.5: "When no leader is heard from"). "First phase" also suggests an election happens once, when Raft actually holds one whenever the leader is lost (the strip: "electing leader after leader").
findings.fix: Raft's way of choosing a leader, run whenever the followers stop hearing from one: the node whose random timeout runs out first starts a new term and asks for votes, and leads once a majority agrees.

findings.quote: while Alan Kay's group worked on the Alto personal computer and Gary Starkweather on the laser printer
findings.problem: This brings back an attribution the book has already corrected. Commit f01c84e (UNDER.md ledger line 3793, 'Alto credited to Thacker and Lampson') rewrote ch8-ethernet-p3 from "Alan Kay's group was inventing the personal computer (the Alto...)" to "Chuck Thacker and Butler Lampson were building the Alto". The tooltip still gives the old attribution, so it contradicts the paragraph beside it.
findings.fix: Xerox's research lab where in 1973 Bob Metcalfe invented Ethernet, while Chuck Thacker and Butler Lampson built the Alto personal computer and Gary Starkweather had already brought the laser printer to life.

findings.quote: Google's JavaScript engine, released with Chrome in 2008, which starts by interpreting code and compiles hot functions to optimised machine code
findings.problem: Putting 'released in 2008' next to 'starts by interpreting' reads as a description of the 2008 engine. The ledger (UNDER.md line 583) corrected exactly that claim: the first V8 had no interpreter and compiled everything straight to machine code, and Ignition only arrived in 2016. ch12-node-p1 and Fig 12.5 now say so, and the tooltip undoes the fix.
findings.fix: Google's JavaScript engine, released with Chrome in 2008. It first compiled everything straight to machine code; today it interprets each function at once and compiles the hot ones to optimised machine code. Node.js runs it outside the browser.

findings.quote: and a finite table of rules; anything computable, it can compute.
findings.problem: A single Turing machine computes only what its own rules say. Fig 1.1's machine adds one, nothing more. The ability to do whatever any machine does belongs to the universal machine, and ch1-context-p5 keeps the two apart. The ledger (line 624) draws the same line: 'a special-purpose computation is still a Turing machine (Fig 1.1's is one), what both lacked was universality'. The tooltip blurs them back together. Read the other way, as a claim about the whole class, it is circular, because 'computable' is defined by Turing machines.
findings.fix: Turing's imaginary computer: an endless tape of cells, a head that reads and writes one cell at a time, and a finite table of rules for each symbol and state. Each machine follows its own rules; the universal machine reads another machine's rules from its tape and does whatever that machine would do.

findings.quote: for two decades the most common web vulnerability
findings.problem: ch12-security-p4 says 'one of the most common web vulnerabilities for two decades running'. The tooltip turns that into 'the most common', which is also false as fact. OWASP ranked XSS first only in 2007 and lower in later editions; its 2021 list puts broken access control first and folds XSS into Injection. CWE's Top 25 put out-of-bounds write above XSS in 2020 to 2023.
findings.fix: Cross-site scripting: injecting attacker script into a site's own pages so it runs with that origin's privileges; for two decades one of the most common web vulnerabilities.

findings.quote: in DNS, how long a resolver may cache an answer.
findings.problem: The term is defined at ch9-ip, but resolvers and DNS caching are not taught until Chapter 11, ch11-dns. A reader at this point has met DNS only as a name in the layer list and does not know what a resolver is or that DNS answers are cached. The defining section explains only the IP meaning.
findings.fix: Time to live: a count in every IP packet that each router lowers by one; the router that brings it to zero drops the packet and reports back, which is how traceroute maps a path. DNS (Chapter 11) uses the same name for how long a saved answer stays valid.

findings.quote: The way every modern computer stores negative numbers
findings.problem: This holds for whole numbers only. The very next section, ch2-float (Fig 2.x, ch2-float-p5), shows negative floating-point numbers stored with a separate sign bit. ch2-twos-p2 itself limits the claim with 'almost never used for whole numbers'.
findings.fix: The way every modern computer stores negative whole numbers: flip every bit of the positive value and add one, so subtraction becomes ordinary addition on the same adder.

findings.quote: from Jim Gray's System R work, used by filesystems and databases.
findings.problem: The term is defined at ch4-fs, but neither Jim Gray nor System R appears anywhere in Part II. Both first come up in Chapter 13. A reader at ch4-fs gets two unexplained names, and the defining section credits the technique only as 'borrowed from database theory'.
findings.fix: Recording each intended change in a log, sealed by a commit record, before applying it, so after a crash committed changes are replayed and the rest discarded; filesystems took the technique from databases (Chapter 13).

findings.quote: that inspect HTTP requests and block SQL-injection-shaped strings before they reach the application.
findings.problem: ch13-injection-p6 says WAFs 'try to spot' injection-shaped strings and that 'None of these alone is sufficient'. The tooltip drops the hedge and presents blocking as certain, which undercuts the paragraph's point. It also suggests WAFs filter SQL injection only, when they screen for many kinds of attack.
findings.fix: Filters, such as Cloudflare's WAF, AWS WAF and ModSecurity, that inspect HTTP requests and try to block attack-shaped input, SQL injection among it, before it reaches the application; one layer of defence, not a fix.

findings.quote: who began Python as a Christmas 1989 hobby at the Centrum Wiskunde & Informatica in Amsterdam
findings.problem: The wording places the hobby work at CWI. ch7-vanrossum-p1 says he worked 'from home' over the holiday break, and his own 1996 foreword agrees: 'My office (a government-run research lab in Amsterdam) would be closed, but I had a home computer' (python.org/doc/essays/foreword/).
findings.fix: Guido van Rossum, a programmer at the Centrum Wiskunde & Informatica in Amsterdam, who began Python at home as a Christmas 1989 hobby and posted it to USENET in 1991.

findings.quote: The static analyser in the Linux kernel
findings.problem: The book never explains 'static analyser'. ch4-security-p15 calls the verifier 'a checker in the kernel that reads every uploaded program', and the tooltip swaps in a term a newcomer cannot unpack.
findings.fix: The checker in the Linux kernel that reads every eBPF program before it loads and refuses it unless it can prove the program always ends, stays within its memory bounds and cannot crash.

findings.quote: The academic security conference on the field's annual circuit
findings.problem: 'The academic security conference' implies there is only one. USENIX Security is one of four top academic security venues, alongside IEEE S&P, ACM CCS and NDSS. The entry also says almost nothing about what the conference is beyond naming its neighbours.
findings.fix: A yearly academic security conference run by the USENIX association, where researchers present peer-reviewed papers; the academic stop on a circuit that also includes DEF CON, Black Hat, CCC and Pwn2Own.

findings.quote: The small set of operators (selection, projection, join, union, difference, cross product, plus rename) that take relations and return a new one; the mathematics under SQL.
findings.problem: This brings back the framing the fact ledger corrected (UNDER.md §4g, Ch13 algebra row: the old prose listed 'σ, π, ⨝, ∪, −, ×, with ρ as a renaming utility'). The entry again lists join as a core operator and adds rename as an extra. The ledger, ch13-algebra-p3 and the Fig 13.2 strip all say the six fundamental operators are σ, π, ∪, −, × and ρ, and that join is derived from a product followed by a selection.
findings.fix: The small set of operators that take relations and return a new one: selection, projection, union, difference, cross product and rename, with the join built from a product and a selection. It is the mathematics under SQL.

findings.quote: A running program together with the private virtual address space the kernel gives it, kept apart from other processes by the MMU's page tables.
findings.problem: The entry's home is ch1-kernel. Pass 29 moved its first use there on purpose, to ch1-kernel-p8. But 'virtual address space', 'MMU' and 'page tables' are first taught in the next section, ch1-memory. The tooltip leans on three terms the reader has not met yet.
findings.fix: A running program as the kernel keeps it: its own memory, its open files and the point it has reached, walled off from every other program.

findings.quote: Public-key systems built on lattice problems or hash functions, not factoring or discrete logarithms, so quantum computers should not break them; NIST published the first standards in 2024.
findings.problem: The entry defines PQC by two of its families, but PQC is defined by resting on problems believed hard for quantum computers (ch14-tls-pqc-p7 says exactly that). Other families exist. In March 2025 NIST picked HQC, which is built on error-correcting codes, as its fifth PQC algorithm (nist.gov/news-events/news/2025/03/nist-selects-hqc-fifth-algorithm-post-quantum-encryption). So 'built on lattice problems or hash functions' is too narrow as a definition.
findings.fix: Public-key systems whose security rests on problems believed hard even for quantum computers, such as lattice problems or hash functions, rather than factoring or discrete logarithms. NIST published the first standards in 2024.

findings.quote: Quick UDP Internet Connections: Google's transport protocol (from around 2012, IETF standard 2021)
findings.problem: The entry gives the expansion as the meaning of the name for the standardised protocol too. RFC 9000 §1.2 says: 'QUIC is a name, not an acronym.' Only Google's original version used the expansion.
findings.fix: Google's transport protocol (from around 2012, IETF standard 2021) that replaces TCP, building reliability, encryption and multiplexing over UDP in user space. Its name first stood for Quick UDP Internet Connections, but the standard treats it as just a name.

findings.quote: The memory ordering a thread puts on an atomic store: every earlier write on that thread is visible by the time the store is.

As written, the entry suggests release alone repairs the x/flag example.
findings.fix: The memory ordering a thread puts on an atomic store: any thread whose acquire load reads that store also sees every write the storing thread made before it.

findings.quote: after a loss its window grows linearly, one segment per round trip.
